results.title: Shop checkout: promo + referral codes can stack without limit

findings.label: discount codes stack (same code twice / total can reach zero or below)
findings.title: Entering the same code repeatedly gives free orders

report.headline: Customers can now stack promo codes, but nothing limits it, so anyone can get a free order by entering codes repeatedly.
what_changed: The checkout used to allow only one promo code per order. It now accepts any number of codes on the same order.
The discounts are added together. For example, the referral code (15% off) plus the spring code (25% off) now gives 40% off.
The same code can be entered more than once, and each entry adds its discount again. This was not part of the stated goal.
The code note says the aim was to let a referral code combine with a seasonal promo. The change allows much more than that: any code combines with any other, including the staff code.
One new automatic test was added to check that the referral and spring codes combine correctly.

risks.title: Entering the same code repeatedly gives free orders
risks.explanation: Nothing stops a customer from entering the same code again and again. Entering the spring code four times takes 100% off. The payment step treats a zero or negative total as a free order and charges nothing. Any customer who tries this gets goods for free. Fix: reject a code that is already on the order, and never let the discount go above the order price.

risks.title: No cap on combined discounts across different codes
risks.explanation: Every code can be stacked with every other code, with no limit on the total. The four current codes together give exactly 100% off, which again means a free order. The staff 50% code can also be combined with customer codes. Fix: allow only the pairing you actually want (one referral code plus one seasonal code), and cap the total discount.

risks.title: Order total can go below zero
risks.explanation: Because discounts are simply added up, the final price can become negative, not just zero. Today this produces a free order rather than a refund. But any receipt, invoice or report that reads this total could show a negative price. The fix above (capping the discount at the order price) solves this too.

questions_for_developer: Which codes should be allowed to combine? Was the plan only one referral code plus one seasonal code, or any codes at all?
Can you block a code that is already on the order, and make sure the total discount can never go above the order price?
Should the staff discount code ever combine with customer codes? If not, can you block that?
Can you add tests that try to apply the same code twice and try stacking all codes, to prove these lead to a sensible price rather than a free order?
good_news: The change is small and only touches the discount part of the cart, so fixing it should be quick.
Invalid codes are still rejected, and the existing tests were updated to match the new behaviour.

results.title: Signup stores passwords in plain text after removing the hashing library

findings.label: passwords stored/compared in plain text
findings.title: All new passwords stored in readable form

report.headline: Passwords are now stored readable and emailed in plain text, and existing customers will be locked out. Do not ship.
what_changed: The app no longer scrambles passwords before saving them. New passwords are stored exactly as people type them.
Login now compares the typed password directly with what is saved, instead of checking it against a scrambled version.
A new 'forgot password' web address emails customers their saved password in plain text.
A new email-sending feature was added, sending from the Habitly address through a mail server named in a setting.
The add-on code that scrambled passwords was removed. The stated reason was that it would not install on the Windows build machine.

risks.title: All new passwords stored in readable form
risks.explanation: From now on, every new customer's password is saved exactly as typed. Anyone who sees the database, a backup or a leaked copy can read every password. Many people reuse passwords, so a leak could expose their email, bank and other accounts too. Bring back proper password scrambling (hashing: a one-way scramble that cannot be reversed) and fix the Windows install problem another way.

risks.title: Every existing customer will be unable to log in
risks.explanation: Existing customers' passwords were saved in scrambled form. Login now compares the typed password with that scrambled text, so it will never match. Every customer who signed up before this change will get 'Wrong email or password'. This breaks the core sign-in flow for your whole current user base.

risks.title: Password emails go out unprotected and can be triggered by anyone
risks.explanation: The new 'forgot password' feature emails the saved password itself. Email is not a safe place for a password, and it may sit in inboxes and mail servers for years. For existing customers it sends scrambled gibberish, which is useless and confusing. Anyone who knows a customer's email can trigger these emails repeatedly, since there is no limit. The standard fix is to email a one-time reset link that expires, never the password.

risks.title: Likely breach of data protection obligations
risks.explanation: Storing passwords readable and emailing them breaks basic security expectations under privacy laws such as GDPR. If there is a leak, this would count against the company with regulators and customers. Fixing the two issues above removes this risk.

risks.title: Forgot-password form demands a password and may crash
risks.explanation: The forgot-password form reuses the login form, so it requires a password, which someone who forgot it does not have. The email setting also defaults to the app's own machine. If no mail server is set up there, the request will fail with an error instead of a friendly message.

questions_for_developer: Can we put back the password scrambling add-on and solve the Windows install problem separately, for example by using a different version or building on another machine?
Can 'forgot password' send a one-time reset link that expires, instead of emailing the password?
Has any version of this change already been published? If so, which accounts were created with readable passwords, and how will we protect them?
Can we limit how often a reset email can be requested for the same address, so it can't be used to spam customers?
good_news: The change is small and has not been committed yet, so it is easy to undo.
The forgot-password feature gives the same reply whether or not the email exists, so it does not reveal who has an account.

results.title: Product search builds SQL from user input (SQL injection)

findings.label: SQL injection in product search/sort
findings.title: Anyone can run their own commands on the database

report.headline: Product search gained category filtering and sorting, but it now lets anyone run their own database commands. Do not ship.
what_changed: Shoppers can now filter product search results by category.
Shoppers can now choose how search results are sorted. Before, results were always sorted by name.
Search results now include each product's category.
When a search fails, the app now sends the full error back to the visitor. That includes the exact database instructions it tried to run.

risks.title: Anyone can run their own commands on the database
risks.explanation: The search box text, the category and the sort choice are now pasted straight into the database instructions. Before this change, the search text was kept separate from them. An attacker can type specially crafted text into the public product search and make the database do things it shouldn't. That includes reading the customer list (emails, full names and payment-provider customer IDs), and possibly changing or deleting data. This is a well-known, easy-to-find attack, so it is very likely to be tried. Ask the developer to keep every visitor-supplied value separate from the database instructions, and to allow only a fixed list of sort options.

risks.title: Customer personal data could leak through product search
risks.explanation: The same database also holds a customers table with emails, full names and payment-provider customer IDs. Because of the flaw above, a stranger could pull those records out through the product search page. A leak like that can trigger data-breach reporting duties under privacy laws such as GDPR, and it would damage customer trust.

risks.title: Error messages show visitors the internal database details
risks.explanation: When a search fails, the app now sends the raw error and the full database instructions back to whoever made the request. This tells an attacker exactly how to adjust their input until the attack works, and it reveals how the database is set up. Errors should show visitors a generic message and keep the details in internal logs.

risks.title: Normal searches with an apostrophe will now fail
risks.explanation: A shopper who searches for something like "men's shoes" will now get an error instead of results. That is because the apostrophe breaks the database instructions. Before this change, that search worked. Fixing the main security problem will also fix this.

questions_for_developer: Can you change the product search so the search text and category are kept separate from the database instructions, the way the old version handled the search text?
Can you limit sorting to a fixed list of allowed options (for example name or price) and ignore anything else a visitor sends?
Can error responses show visitors a generic message and keep the technical details in our internal logs only?
Has this version been published anywhere public? If so, can we check the database logs for any unusual searches?
good_news: The change only touches product search, so fixing it is a small, contained job.
The new filter and sorting features are reasonable and can be kept once they are built safely.

results.title: Checkout retries card charges without an idempotency key (double charge)

findings.label: retrying a charge can bill the customer twice
findings.title: Customers can be charged up to four times for one order

report.headline: Checkout now retries failed card payments up to four times, but removed double-charge protection, so customers can be charged several times for one order.
what_changed: When the payment company is slow or returns an error, checkout now tries the card payment again, up to 4 attempts in total, waiting a little longer each time.
The protection against charging the same order twice was removed. This is a unique order tag sent with each payment, which the payment company uses to ignore repeat charges.
The payment description on each charge now includes the date and time of that attempt, so every retry looks like a new, different charge.
A new shared helper was added for retrying. It retries after any error at all, not only network problems.

risks.title: Customers can be charged up to four times for one order
risks.explanation: Before this change, every payment for an order carried the same order tag, so the payment company would never charge it twice. That tag has been removed. Now, if the payment company is slow (more than 8 seconds), our app gives up waiting and tries again, even though the first charge may already have gone through. Because the change was made for times when the payment company is busy, this will very likely happen under heavy load. The result is duplicate charges, refunds, chargebacks and angry customers. Put the order tag back before shipping. With the tag in place, retrying is safe.

risks.title: Declined cards are retried, so checkout gets much slower
risks.explanation: The retry runs after every kind of error, including a declined card or invalid details, which will never succeed on a retry. Each attempt can wait up to 8 seconds, plus the pauses between attempts. A customer could stare at a spinning checkout for about 35 seconds before seeing an error. Repeated attempts on a declined card can also look suspicious to card companies' fraud checks. Only retry on genuine timeouts or connection problems.

questions_for_developer: Why was the order tag that stops double charges removed? Can we restore it so the payment company ignores repeat charges for the same order?
Why does each payment description now include the time? Can we remove that so every retry for an order stays identical?
Can retries happen only when the payment company times out or can't be reached, and not when a card is declined?
What is the longest a customer could wait on the checkout page before seeing a result? Can we cap it at a few seconds?
good_news: The goal is reasonable. Retrying when the payment company is briefly slow can rescue real sales once double-charge protection is back.
The change is small and limited to the checkout payment step, so it is quick to fix.

results.title: Migration drops users.phone while SMS reminders still read it

findings.label: dropping phone column deletes data and breaks SMS reminders that still use it
findings.title: Appointment text reminders will stop sending entirely

report.headline: This change deletes every patient's phone number from the database, but the appointment text reminders still need those numbers, so they will stop working.
what_changed: The phone number column is removed from the user records in the database. Every stored phone number is erased when this is published.
The app's description of a user no longer includes a phone number.
A note says the numbers have moved to a new customer system (ticket CL-212). Nothing in this code reads numbers from that new system.

risks.title: Appointment text reminders will stop sending entirely
risks.explanation: The reminder job texts patients 24 hours before their appointment, and it still looks up each patient's phone number. That number no longer exists, so the job will crash on the first patient who has opted in. No reminders go out, which likely means more missed appointments. Keep the phone number until the reminder job reads numbers from the new customer system.

risks.title: All phone numbers erased with no way to undo
risks.explanation: Publishing this permanently deletes every patient's phone number. The 'undo' step for this database change is empty, so it cannot bring the numbers back. Unless someone has confirmed every number really is in the new customer system and a backup exists, this data is lost. Confirm the copy is complete before you publish.

risks.title: Phone number updates from patients silently thrown away
risks.explanation: The screen where patients update their contact details still accepts a phone number. After this change, the number is quietly ignored and never saved anywhere, and no error is shown. Patients will think they updated their number when they did not. Either remove the phone field there or send it to the new customer system.

questions_for_developer: The appointment text reminders still read the patient's phone number from our database. How will they get numbers after this change? Can we hold this change until they read from the new customer system?
Has someone confirmed that every phone number is already in the new customer system (ticket CL-212)? Do we have a backup taken before this runs?
The 'undo' step for this database change does nothing. Can it at least re-create the empty phone column, so the app can be rolled back?
What should happen when a patient changes their phone number on the contact details screen now? Right now it would be silently ignored.
good_news: The change is small and easy to hold back. Nothing has been published yet, so no data has been lost.
The reminder code still checks each patient's text-message opt-in, so consent handling itself was not weakened.

results.title: Live payment secret key hard-coded and .env.production committed

findings.label: live secret key committed to the code
findings.title: Live Stripe secret key written into the code

report.headline: This change puts your live Stripe payment key into the code and the shared files, so do not ship it as it stands.
what_changed: A new settings file was added. It holds your live Stripe secret key (the master password to your Stripe account), your public Stripe key and your site address.
The rule that kept settings files like this out of the shared project history was removed. The new file will now be saved and shared with everyone who can see the code.
The checkout code now has the live secret key typed directly into it. It uses that key whenever the key setting is missing, for example on preview (test) versions of the site.
Before this change, the app refused to start if the key was missing. Now it quietly falls back to taking real payments with your live account, even on test versions.

risks.title: Live Stripe secret key written into the code
risks.explanation: Your live Stripe secret key now sits in plain text in two places. Anyone who can see the code can use it to take money, issue refunds, read customer payment details or change your account. That includes any developer, contractor or tool with access, and the whole internet if the code is ever public. Treat the key as leaked: create a new key in Stripe, cancel the old one, and remove it from both files before saving them.

risks.title: Safety rule protecting secret files was removed
risks.explanation: The project had a rule stopping settings files with secrets from being saved into shared history. This change deletes that rule. So this file, and any future one like it, will be saved and copied wherever the code goes. Once a secret is in the history, deleting the file later does not remove it. Put the rule back.

risks.title: Test versions of the site will take real payments
risks.explanation: Preview (test) versions of the site will now use your live account instead of failing. Anyone testing checkout there, staff included, will be charged real money. Those test orders will also mix with your real sales records. Preview versions should use Stripe's test key, set as a setting on the hosting service, and never fall back to the live key.

questions_for_developer: Can you create a new Stripe secret key, cancel the old one, and confirm the old one no longer works, since it is now in the code?
Can you remove the key from the checkout code and the new settings file, and put back the rule that keeps settings files out of the shared code?
Can you fix the preview (test) versions by adding Stripe's test key as a setting on the hosting service, so they never use the live account?
Has this code been pushed or shared anywhere yet? If so, the key is in that copy's history and must be treated as public.
good_news: The live secret key is only used by the server-side checkout code, not the pages customers' browsers load, so it is not sent to visitors directly.
The real problem, preview versions failing, is simple to fix the right way by adding a setting on the hosting service.

results.title: New admin API route (delete user / change role) has no admin check

findings.label: admin delete/role-change route reachable without being an admin
findings.title: Anyone can make themselves admin or delete any user

report.headline: The admin Users screen can now change roles and delete users, but anyone on the internet can do both without logging in.
what_changed: On the admin Users screen, each person now has a dropdown to set their role: member, manager or admin.
Each person also has a Delete button. It asks for confirmation, then removes the user and all their shifts.
Two new web addresses the app answers were added behind the scenes. One changes a user's role and one deletes a user.

risks.title: Anyone can make themselves admin or delete any user
risks.explanation: The existing "list users" address checks that the caller is a logged-in admin. The two new addresses skip that check entirely. The login guard on the admin pages covers only the screens, not these addresses. So anyone who knows a user's ID can promote any account to admin or delete accounts, with no login at all. Ask the developer to add the same admin check the list uses before shipping.

risks.title: Deleting a user permanently wipes all their shifts
risks.explanation: The database is set up so that deleting a user also deletes every shift they worked. There is no undo, and it is not a soft delete (hiding instead of erasing). Combined with the missing login check, an outsider could erase staff and shift history. Even for real admins, one wrong click loses work records that may be needed for payroll or disputes. Consider keeping shift history, or archiving users instead of erasing them.

risks.title: Role can be set to any made-up value
risks.explanation: The screen offers three roles, but the server accepts whatever text it is sent. Someone could save a role like "superadmin" or a blank value. That could lock a person out or confuse later permission checks. The server should only accept member, manager or admin.

risks.title: Failures are silent on the admin screen
risks.explanation: If a role change or delete fails, the screen shows no error. The admin may think it worked when it did not. The list does reload afterwards, so the true state does show up, but there is no message explaining why.

questions_for_developer: The new change-role and delete-user addresses don't check that the caller is a logged-in admin, unlike the existing user list. Can you add the same admin check to both before we ship?
Can the server reject any role other than member, manager or admin?
Should deleting a user really erase all of their shift history? Or should we archive the user and keep the shifts for payroll and records?
What stops an admin from accidentally removing their own admin role or deleting themselves, so that no admin is left?
good_news: The change is small and easy to fix. The admin check already exists in the code and just needs to be reused here.
The Delete button asks for confirmation before removing anyone.

results.title: Debug middleware logs full request bodies (SSN, card numbers) to a third-party log service

findings.label: personal/payment data written to logs (shipped to log provider)
findings.title: SSNs and bank account numbers sent to outside log service

report.headline: New request logging copies every loan applicant's Social Security number and bank details to an outside log service. Do not ship.
what_changed: Every visit to the app is now written to the logs in full. That includes everything the customer typed and the extra information their browser sent.
The stated goal is to help debug the problem with failed loan applications.
The logs already go to an outside company (Better Stack's Logtail), which keeps them for 30 days. So this new detail goes there too.
No other features or screens were changed.

risks.title: SSNs and bank account numbers sent to outside log service
risks.explanation: The loan application form collects the owner's full name, Social Security number, date of birth, bank account number and routing number. The new logging records the whole form, so every one of these goes in plain text to the outside log service and stays there for 30 days. This happens to every applicant, every time, starting the moment it ships. It is a likely breach of data-protection rules for lenders (for example US financial privacy rules and state breach laws), and anyone with access to the logs could steal identities. Log only safe details (which page, how long it took, the result), or hide the sensitive fields before logging.

risks.title: Login passwords and session details also copied into logs
risks.explanation: The logging also records all the extra information sent with each request. That normally includes login tokens and cookies (the details that prove who a user is). Anyone who can read the logs could use these to act as a logged-in customer or staff member. Leave this extra information out of the logs, or keep only a few harmless items.

risks.title: Every request may wait on the outside log service
risks.explanation: The existing log setup sends each log line to the outside service and waits up to 2 seconds for an answer. The new logging runs on every request, in a part of the app that cannot do other work while it waits. If the log service is slow, the whole app could slow down for all customers, including people submitting applications. Ask the developer to send logs in the background so customers never wait on them.

questions_for_developer: Can you change the logging so it never records Social Security numbers, dates of birth, bank account or routing numbers, or login details? Can you show me a sample log line to confirm?
Has any version of this already run anywhere (a test server or production)? If so, can we delete those logs from the outside log service and check whether we must report it?
Can we debug the failed applications by logging only the page, the result and the error message, instead of the full form?
Can logs be sent to the outside service in the background, so a slow log service never slows down customers?
good_news: The change is small and easy to undo. It is one new file plus two lines that switch it on.
The existing application page was careful to log only the business name and amount. Following that same approach would fix the main problem.

results.title: Ticket-summary job re-summarises every ticket every minute with unbounded retries/recursion

findings.label: AI bill can blow up (every ticket every minute, unlimited retries/recursion)
findings.title: Every ticket is sent to paid AI every minute

report.headline: New AI ticket summaries would re-summarize every ticket, every minute, likely costing a fortune and overloading the system. Don't ship yet.
what_changed: Adds a background job that sends each support ticket's full conversation to OpenAI (a paid AI service) and saves a short summary for the inbox preview.
Schedules this job to run every minute, all day, every day.
Each run covers every ticket ever created, including closed ones, not just new or changed tickets.
If a summary is longer than about 280 characters, the job asks the AI to shorten it again, with no limit on how many times it tries.
If the AI service returns an error, the job retries straight away, forever, with no pause.

risks.title: Every ticket is sent to paid AI every minute
risks.explanation: The inbox has about 40,000 open tickets, plus every closed one. All of them are re-summarized every minute, even when nothing has changed. That adds up to tens of millions of paid AI requests a day and could easily run into thousands of dollars daily. Only summarize tickets that are new or have new messages, and run it far less often.

risks.title: Errors cause endless, instant retries
risks.explanation: When the AI service fails or says 'slow down', the job tries again immediately, forever, with no wait and no limit. During an outage or rate limit, this hammers the service, keeps the worker busy, and can rack up more charges. Add a short pause between retries, a maximum number of attempts, and let a ticket simply fail until the next run.

risks.title: All tickets processed at once, and runs pile up
risks.explanation: The job fires off requests for every ticket at the same moment, which will hit the AI service's limits and strain the database. A full run cannot finish within one minute, so a new run starts on top of the old one, again and again. This can slow or crash the worker that also closes stale tickets. Process tickets in small batches and stop a new run starting while one is still going.

risks.title: Customer conversations now shared with OpenAI
risks.explanation: Full support conversations, which may include names, emails or other personal details, are now sent to an outside company. Your customer contracts or privacy policy may need to list OpenAI as a data processor. Confirm this is allowed before turning it on.

risks.title: Shortening step can loop with no limit
risks.explanation: If the AI keeps returning summaries over 280 characters, the job keeps asking it to shorten them, with no cap. Very long conversations are also sent in full, which costs more and can be rejected for being too large, triggering the endless retry above. Cap the number of shortening attempts and trim very long conversations first.

questions_for_developer: Can the job only summarize tickets that are new or got a new message since their last summary, and skip closed tickets?
How often do inbox previews really need refreshing? Could it run every 15 minutes or hourly instead of every minute?
Can we add a spending limit on the OpenAI account and a cap on retries, with a pause between them, so a failure can't run up a big bill?
Do our privacy policy and customer agreements allow sending support conversations to OpenAI, and should we remove personal details first?
good_news: The change is small and kept to one new job, so it is easy to fix or switch off.
Summaries are saved to the database in a safe way that keeps the data separate from the database instructions.

results.title: Renewals moved to customer-local midnight; mixed time zones cause double/missed charges

findings.label: time-zone mix-up bills some customers twice (and skips day-31 renewals)
findings.title: Customers outside the server's time zone can be charged twice

report.headline: Renewals now aim for midnight in each customer's time zone, but the change can double-charge customers and skip others entirely.
what_changed: Subscription renewals are meant to charge customers at midnight in their own time zone, not the company's.
The system no longer tracks a set 'next renewal date' for each subscription. It now checks whether today's calendar day matches the day the customer signed up.
The protection against charging the same renewal twice now changes every hour. It used to be tied to the renewal date.
The old rule that moved the 29th, 30th and 31st to the last day of shorter months is no longer used.

risks.title: Customers outside the server's time zone can be charged twice
risks.explanation: To avoid billing twice, the system compares the customer's local date with the server's date. For most customers these differ for part of the day. For example, a Los Angeles customer's renewal day continues after the server's clock has already moved to the next day. If the billing job runs more than once a day, which a 'midnight in each time zone' design needs, it will charge that customer a second time. The duplicate-charge protection now changes every hour, so the payment provider will not block the repeat charge either.

questions_for_developer: How often will the billing job run after this change? If it runs every hour, can a Los Angeles or Tokyo customer be charged twice on their renewal day? The 'already billed today' check uses the server's date, not the customer's.
Customers who signed up on the 29th, 30th or 31st: when will they be billed in February and in 30-day months? The old rule that moved them to the month's last day seems to be gone.
If the billing job is down on a customer's renewal day, does that customer still get billed later, or do we lose that month's payment?
If a charge goes through but saving the record then fails, could the retry an hour later charge the customer again? The protection against double charges now changes every hour.
good_news: The change is small and only touches the renewal logic, so it is easy to fix or undo.
Each subscription already stores the customer's time zone, so the goal of billing on 'their' day can be met without changing how the database is organised.

results.title: Marketing copy edits and typo fixes

report.headline: Spelling fixes and new button wording on the home and pricing pages; safe to ship, with one small wording point to check.
what_changed: Fixed spelling on the home page: "patern" is now "pattern" and "attachements" is now "attachments".
Fixed spelling on the pricing page: "hobbiests" is now "hobbyists", and "14 day free trail" is now "14-day free trial".
The sign-up buttons on the home page and on every pricing plan now say "Start your free trial" instead of "Get started free". This goes beyond fixing typos.
Small wording tweaks: "scans" is now "scanned pages", and the Guild plan says "several locations" instead of "many locations".
The buttons still go to the same sign-up pages, so how people sign up has not changed.

risks.title: "Free trial" button on a plan that is already free
risks.explanation: The Starter plan costs $0, but its button now says "Start your free trial". A visitor may think the free plan ends or starts charging after the trial. This could cause some confusion or put off a few sign-ups, but it doesn't affect billing. Think about keeping "Get started free" on the Starter plan only.

questions_for_developer: Does the sign-up flow really start a 14-day trial for every plan, including the free Starter plan? The buttons now promise a "free trial".
Can the Starter plan's button keep saying "Get started free", since that plan never charges?
good_news: Only on-screen wording changed. Prices, plan features and sign-up links are exactly the same.
I found no other place in the project that relies on the old button text, so nothing else should break.
The spelling fixes make the pages look more professional to visitors.

results.title: Refactor: extract duplicated money formatting into a helper (no behaviour change)

report.headline: An internal tidy-up of how invoice amounts are shown; invoices should look exactly the same, and it is safe to ship.
what_changed: The step that turns amounts into text like "$1,234.50" now lives in one shared place. Before, it was copied in two places.
Invoice line items and invoice totals now use that same shared step, so they cannot drift apart later.
The way amounts are rounded and shown has not changed. Customers should see identical invoices.
A new automatic check was added. It confirms that dollar, euro and other currency amounts display correctly, including currencies without a symbol (for example "CHF 12.00").
The developer also added labels to the code that describe what kind of information each part expects. Users won't notice this.
questions_for_developer: Did the existing invoice checks pass after this change? They compare a full sample invoice, including the total, against the exact expected text.
good_news: The change is small and limited to how invoices are displayed. It does not touch payments or customer data.
I searched the whole project. The one part whose inputs changed is used in only one place, and that place was updated to match.
The existing invoice checks still cover the full invoice text, and a new check was added for the shared amount step.

results.title: Add a /healthz endpoint for the load balancer

report.headline: This adds a simple "are you alive?" check for the load balancer, and it is safe to ship as is.
what_changed: The app now answers a new web address that the load balancer (the system that sends traffic to the right server) can check. It replies "ok" plus the app's version number, currently 4.1.2.
The README now lists this health check and the existing parcel-status address.
A new automatic test checks that the health check answers correctly.
Parcel tracking for customers is unchanged.

risks.title: Test will fail at the next version bump
risks.explanation: The new test expects the version number to be exactly 4.1.2. When someone raises the version, this test will fail even though nothing is broken. This won't affect customers, but it could slow down a future release until someone updates the test.

risks.title: Anyone can see which app version is running
risks.explanation: The health check is public and shows the exact version number. That gives attackers a small hint about which known bugs might apply. The risk is minor for a tracking app like this. If you'd rather not share it, the version can be left out or kept to internal traffic only.

questions_for_developer: The health check always says "ok" once the app is running. Is that enough for the load balancer, or should it also confirm that parcel lookups actually work?
Can the test check that the version matches the project's settings file, instead of a fixed number, so it doesn't break at the next release?
good_news: The change is small and kept separate from the rest. It touches no customer data, payments or logins.
The existing parcel-tracking behaviour is unchanged, and the new feature has its own test.
No add-on code from other companies or projects was added.

results.title: Add a dark-mode toggle (preference saved in the browser)

report.headline: Adds a dark mode button to the Recipe Box header that remembers each visitor's choice; small, safe, and fine to ship.
what_changed: A new button in the header next to the search box switches the site between light and dark colours.
The site remembers each visitor's choice on their own device, so it stays the same next time they visit.
First-time visitors get the colour scheme their phone or computer already prefers.
Colour changes now fade in smoothly instead of switching instantly.
All buttons on the site now get a simple outlined style. Right now this is the only button, so nothing else changes.

risks.title: Site could fail to load if browser blocks saved settings
risks.explanation: The app reads and saves the colour choice using the browser's small on-device storage. A few browsers block this storage when the strictest privacy settings are on. For those visitors the page may show up blank instead of just skipping the saved choice. This affects very few people, and a developer can fix it in a few minutes.

risks.title: Search box and page may briefly look wrong in dark mode
risks.explanation: The search box has no dark colours of its own. In dark mode it may stay bright white against the dark page. Visitors who chose dark mode may also see a quick white flash as the page loads. Both are cosmetic and nothing breaks.

questions_for_developer: If a visitor's browser blocks saved settings (some strict privacy modes do), does the site still load? Can we make it fall back to light mode instead?
Can you check the search box and recipe cards in dark mode on a phone and a laptop so everything is easy to read?
good_news: The change is small and touches only appearance. No customer data, payments or accounts are involved.
The saved choice stays only on the visitor's own device and is never sent anywhere.
The button is labelled for screen readers, so visitors with poor or no sight can use it.

results.title: Add 'download my invoices as CSV' (properly scoped to the signed-in customer)

report.headline: Customers can now download their own invoices as a spreadsheet file, and each customer only gets their own invoices.
what_changed: Signed-in customers get a new download link in the portal. It gives them a spreadsheet file (CSV) of all their invoices, ready to send to their accountant.
The file lists the invoice number, issue date, total in normal currency format (for example 199.00), and status (paid, open or void). Newest invoices come first.
The existing invoice list works the same as before. The developer moved its database lookup into one shared piece that both the list and the download now use.
A small automatic test was added for the download.

risks.title: The new test checks very little
risks.explanation: The test only checks that the reply is marked as a spreadsheet file. It never checks what is inside the file, such as the header row or the amounts. If someone later breaks the contents, for example by showing totals wrong, the test would still pass. Ask the developer to make the test check the actual rows.

questions_for_developer: Can you extend the new test so it checks the file's contents, such as the header row and a total showing as 199.00, not just the file type?
Should cancelled ('void') invoices be in the accountant's spreadsheet, or should they be left out or marked more clearly?
good_news: The download uses the same sign-in check and the same 'only this customer's invoices' filter as the existing invoice list. One customer cannot download another customer's invoices.
The change is small and contained. The existing invoice list behaves exactly as it did before.
Amounts are converted from cents to normal currency with two decimal places, which is what an accountant will expect.

results.title: Partial refunds from support dashboard: remaining-balance check dropped (buried in a mixed diff)

findings.label: support can refund more than the customer paid / refund the same order repeatedly
findings.title: Agents can refund more than the member paid

report.headline: Partial refunds were added, but the safety checks against refunding more than the member paid were removed. Don't ship yet.
what_changed: Support agents can now refund part of an order, such as one missed class, by typing an amount. Leaving the amount empty refunds whatever is left.
The refund button now says "Refund" instead of "Refund order". A new label explains the amount box.
The "refund sent" and "order not found" messages were reworded to be clearer.
The internal refund log now shows amounts in dollars (e.g. "$19.99") instead of raw cents.
The README gained a short section on refunds. A small formatting helper was tidied up but works the same.

risks.title: Agents can refund more than the member paid
risks.explanation: Before, the system refused to refund an order that was already fully refunded. That check was deleted, and the typed amount is never compared with what is left. An agent could refund $50 on a $20 order, refund the same order twice, or enter a zero or negative amount. Before shipping, ask the developer to reject any amount that is zero, negative, or more than the money still unrefunded.

risks.title: Double-clicking Refund can now send two refunds
risks.explanation: Each refund carries a tag that tells the card processor "this is the same request, don't do it twice". The old tag was the same every time for a given order, so repeat clicks or retries were ignored. The new tag includes the current time, so every click looks like a brand-new refund. A double-click, slow network retry, or two agents working the same ticket could pay the member twice. The developer should use a tag that stays the same for the same refund attempt.

risks.title: Refund records can show more refunded than paid
risks.explanation: Because nothing caps the amount, the order record can end up saying more was refunded than was paid. The "refund the rest" option would then calculate a negative amount. This makes the books wrong and can confuse later refunds or reports. Fixing the amount check above also fixes this.

questions_for_developer: Can you add a check that blocks any refund that is zero, negative, or bigger than the amount still left to refund on the order?
Can you bring back protection against sending the same refund twice (for example if an agent double-clicks), instead of tagging each refund with the current time?
Does our card processor itself block refunds above the original charge, or are we relying only on our own app for that?
Can we add a few tests for partial refunds: two partial refunds in a row, an amount too large, and refunding an already fully refunded order?
good_news: The change is small and limited to the refund feature, so it's quick to fix.
The text changes for support staff are clearer and set more accurate expectations ("business days").
The log now shows refund amounts in a readable dollar format and still records which agent made the refund.

results.title: New invoice PDF download checks login but not ownership (any customer can read any invoice)

findings.label: any signed-in customer can download other customers' invoices by changing the number
findings.title: Any customer can download any other customer's invoice

report.headline: Customers can now download invoices as PDFs, but any logged-in customer can download anyone else's invoice.
what_changed: Adds a "download as PDF" option for invoices, so customers can forward them to their accountant.
The PDF shows the invoice number, issue date, total and the billing email address.
The invoice list now includes each invoice's internal ID number. The new download link uses this number.

risks.title: Any customer can download any other customer's invoice
risks.explanation: The new download address checks that someone is logged in. It never checks that the invoice belongs to them. Invoice ID numbers simply count up (1, 2, 3…), so a logged-in customer can change the number in the link and download every invoice in the system. Each PDF reveals another customer's email address, invoice amounts and dates. That is a personal data leak, which may need reporting under privacy laws such as GDPR. Fix this before shipping: only return the invoice if it belongs to the logged-in customer, the same way the existing invoice list already does.

risks.title: Some invoices may produce broken or unreadable PDFs
risks.explanation: The PDF is built by hand. Brackets in the invoice text are not handled, and the line breaks may not show up as separate lines. The file also leaves out some parts that PDF readers normally expect, such as a font and an index of its contents. Some PDF viewers or accounting tools may show a blank page or refuse to open it. Ask the developer to test the files in several common PDF viewers, or to use a standard PDF-making tool.

questions_for_developer: Can you make the PDF download refuse (with a 'not found' message) any invoice that doesn't belong to the logged-in customer, and add a test that proves customer A can't download customer B's invoice?
Has this download been live anywhere yet? If so, can we check the server records for people downloading invoices that aren't theirs?
Have you opened the generated PDFs in common viewers (Adobe, Chrome, Mac Preview) and checked that the lines display correctly?
good_news: The change is small and contained, so the fix for the main problem is a one-line ownership check.
The existing invoice list still correctly shows each customer only their own invoices.

results.title: Refactor payment client into a module with typed errors (behaviour and double-charge protection unchanged)

report.headline: This is a behind-the-scenes tidy-up of how checkout charges cards. Payments should work exactly as before, so it is safe to ship.
what_changed: Customers will see no difference on the checkout page. They are charged the same amount, in US dollars, with the same order description.
The protection against charging a customer twice for the same order is still in place and works as it did before.
When the card payment company rejects a request, the error is now labelled more clearly. Developers can more easily tell payment failures apart from other problems.
The code that prepares each charge and its security details was split into smaller pieces. It does the same thing as before.
The saved change note says the payment code was moved into a new folder. No files were actually moved. The note slightly overstates the change, but nothing is broken.
questions_for_developer: The change note says the payment code moved into a new folder, but it did not move. Was that move planned and left out, or is the note just inaccurate?
good_news: The change is small and limited to the payment code. I checked the code that uses it, and nothing else depends on what changed.
The charge amount, currency and protection against double charges are all unchanged.
Failed orders are still marked as failed, just as before.

results.title: Add an optional 'marketing emails' preference column (off by default) with a safe migration

report.headline: This adds a newsletter opt-in for patients that starts switched off for everyone. It is safe to ship.
what_changed: Each patient record now has a yes/no setting for whether they want the clinic newsletter.
Every patient starts at "no". That covers existing patients and new sign-ups. Nobody is signed up without choosing it.
The app can now save a patient's newsletter choice. No button or profile page uses this yet, so patients won't see anything new.
The database gets one new column (a change to how the database is organised). Nothing is removed or renamed, and the change can be undone cleanly.
Nothing sends a newsletter yet. This change only prepares for one.

risks.title: The app doesn't record when or how consent was given
risks.explanation: The app saves only yes or no. It doesn't save when the patient agreed or what wording they saw. Under privacy laws like GDPR, the clinic may need to prove consent if someone complains. Consider recording the date and wording before the first newsletter goes out.

questions_for_developer: When we build the newsletter sending, will it only email patients who said yes? Will every email have an unsubscribe link that switches this setting back to no?
Should we also save the date a patient opted in, and the wording they agreed to, so we can prove consent later?
Where will patients see this choice on their profile page? Will it check that they can only change their own setting?
good_news: Everyone starts opted out, existing patients included. That is the safe, privacy-friendly default.
The change is small and only adds things. It doesn't touch the existing text-message reminders or their opt-out.
The database change can be undone without affecting any other data.

results.title: Big diff (vendored 400 KB chart library) hides a public, unauthenticated customer export

findings.label: customer export (emails, phones, spend) downloadable by anyone without signing in
findings.title: Full customer list downloadable by anyone, no sign-in

report.headline: This adds a sales chart and a customer list download, but anyone on the internet can download the full customer list without signing in.
what_changed: The main page now shows a space for a monthly spending chart and a "Download customer list" link.
A new download gives every customer's name, email, phone, birthday and total lifetime spend as a spreadsheet file.
A new web address the app answers gives monthly sales totals across all orders.
Chart-drawing add-on code (labelled "chartkit") was copied straight into the website files instead of being installed from a known source.

risks.title: Full customer list downloadable by anyone, no sign-in
risks.explanation: The existing customer pages require staff to sign in first. The new reports section skips that check. Anyone who visits the download link gets every customer's name, email, phone, birthday and spending. The link is shown on the public front page, so finding it is easy. That is a personal data breach you may have to report under privacy laws such as GDPR. Have the developer add the same staff sign-in check before publishing.

risks.title: Company sales figures are also public
risks.explanation: The monthly sales totals use the same unprotected setup. Anyone, including competitors, can see your revenue month by month. The same sign-in fix covers this.

risks.title: Unverified chart add-on code with an unclear origin
risks.explanation: A large, scrambled file of chart code was added directly to the site, and it loads for every visitor. I found no signs of it sending data elsewhere. But its contents look like meaningless filler rather than a real charting tool, and nothing on the page uses it yet. Ask where it came from and replace it with an official, checkable copy, or remove it.

risks.title: Spreadsheet can break on names containing commas
risks.explanation: Customer details are joined with commas, with no protection. A name like "Smith, Jane" will shift columns and confuse your accountant's file. Also, a value starting with "=" could run as a formula when opened in Excel. Ask the developer to format the file properly.

questions_for_developer: Can you put the same staff sign-in check on the new reports section that the customer pages already use, and confirm the download fails when signed out?
Where did the chartkit file come from? Can we use an official, verified copy instead, since this file looks scrambled and nothing uses it yet?
Does the accountant really need customers' birthdays and phone numbers, or can we leave those out of the download?
Can the spreadsheet handle commas and quote marks in names, and block values that Excel would treat as formulas?
good_news: The change is small and easy to fix: one missing sign-in check is the main problem.
The database instructions are fixed text and don't include anything visitors type, so they can't be tampered with that way.

results.title: Win-back email script runs on every deploy and ignores unsubscribes

findings.label: the email goes out again on every deploy (several times a day)
findings.title: Inactive customers get the same email several times daily

findings.label: people who unsubscribed still get marketing email (consent / anti-spam law)
findings.title: Emails people who unsubscribed

report.headline: A new 40%-off "we miss you" email goes out on every release, ignoring unsubscribes. Do not ship as is.
what_changed: Adds a win-back email campaign. It offers 40% off the next course with one shared discount code.
The email goes to every user inactive for 30+ days, plus every user with no activity on record.
The campaign is attached to the automatic steps that run after each release. Per the README, releases happen several times a day.
There is no schedule, no record of who already got the email, and no unsubscribe link in the message.

risks.title: Inactive customers get the same email several times daily
risks.explanation: The email is sent as part of every release, and the README says releases happen several times a day. Nothing records who already received it. So every inactive user, possibly tens of thousands of the ~120k registered, gets the same promotion again after each release. This will annoy customers, drive unsubscribes and spam complaints, and can get the company's sending address blocked by email providers. Move the campaign out of the release process into a separately scheduled job that remembers who was already emailed.

risks.title: Emails people who unsubscribed
risks.explanation: The users table has an unsubscribed date field, but the new code never checks it when picking recipients. People who opted out will still get marketing emails, which breaks anti-spam and privacy laws such as CAN-SPAM and GDPR and can bring complaints or fines. The email also has no unsubscribe link, which CAN-SPAM requires for marketing messages. Exclude unsubscribed users and add an unsubscribe link before any send.

risks.title: One failed email can break the release and cause repeats
risks.explanation: If the email service rejects a single message, the whole script stops partway through. The after-release step then reports a failure, even though the release itself was fine. Anyone who retries the release resends the email to everyone already reached before the failure. The script should skip and log individual failures rather than stop.

risks.title: Shared 40% code with no limits
risks.explanation: Every recipient gets the same code, and the email does not mention any limit on who can use it. If the checkout accepts it for anyone, it can be shared online and used by active, full-paying customers. Confirm the code is restricted to the intended people or to one use per account.

questions_for_developer: Can we run the win-back email as its own scheduled job (for example weekly), not as part of every release, and keep a record of who already got it so nobody receives it twice?
Can you exclude anyone with an unsubscribed date from this email and add a working unsubscribe link to the message?
Users with no activity on record are also included. Does that mean everyone who signed up but never logged in, even years ago? Is that who we want to email?
Is the COMEBACK40 code limited to one use per account and to these inactive users, or can anyone who finds it use it?
good_news: The change is small and easy to undo. Removing the one added step from the release process stops all sending.
The database instructions keep data separate from the commands, so they can't be tampered with.

results.title: Gift-card purchase passes a dollar amount where the gateway expects cents (charges 100x too little)

findings.label: gift cards charged in dollars as if cents: a $50 card costs 50 cents
findings.title: Gift cards charged in cents instead of dollars

report.headline: New gift card purchase charges buyers about one hundredth of the price, so a $100 card costs $1. Don't ship yet.
what_changed: Customers can now buy a BrewBox gift card ($25, $50 or $100) for someone else.
The buyer's card is charged, and the buyer gets a gift code back.
The README now has a short note describing gift card purchases.
The recipient's email address is collected, but no email is sent to them yet.

risks.title: Gift cards charged in cents instead of dollars
risks.explanation: The gift card price list stores amounts in dollars (25, 50, 100). The payment system expects cents. So a $25 card charges 25 cents, and a $100 card charges $1. Every gift card sold would lose almost all its value. The developer needs to convert dollars to cents (multiply by 100) or store prices in cents before this ships.

risks.title: Gift codes are never saved, so they can't be redeemed
risks.explanation: The code is created and handed back, but it isn't recorded anywhere. Nothing in the app can later check that a code is real or how much it's worth. Buyers would pay for a card the recipient can't use, which leads to refunds and complaints. Ask the developer how codes get stored and redeemed.

risks.title: Double-charge protection doesn't work on retries
risks.explanation: The protection against charging the same purchase twice is tied to a brand new random code made on each attempt. If the buyer clicks twice, or the connection drops and the purchase is retried, the payment company sees it as a new purchase. The buyer could be charged twice for one card. Regular orders tie this protection to a fixed order number; gift cards should do the same.

risks.title: Recipient is never told about their gift
risks.explanation: The recipient's email is taken but no email is sent. Unless something else handles it, the person receiving the gift won't hear about it. Confirm who delivers the code.

questions_for_developer: The gift card prices are stored in dollars, but the payment system expects cents. Can you fix it so a $25 card actually charges $25, and add a check that proves it?
Where is each gift code saved, and how does the shop check a code and its balance when someone tries to use it?
If a buyer clicks 'buy' twice or the connection drops, what stops them being charged twice? Can you tie the double-charge protection to a fixed purchase number instead of a fresh random code?
Who sends the gift code to the recipient's email, and when?
good_news: The change is small and kept to its own new file, so it doesn't alter the existing coffee checkout.
Gift codes are made with a strong random generator, so they are hard to guess.

results.title: Single-use coupon checked then marked used in separate steps (can be redeemed many times in parallel)

findings.label: the same single-use coupon can be redeemed several times by simultaneous requests
findings.title: A single-use $100 coupon can be redeemed several times

report.headline: Customers can now apply partner coupons to orders, but one "single-use" $100 coupon can be used several times by sending quick repeat requests.
what_changed: Adds a new web address the app answers so a coupon code can be applied to a ticket order.
The app looks up the code, checks it hasn't been used, takes its amount off the order, then marks the coupon as used.
Codes are tidied before checking: extra spaces are removed and letters are made uppercase, so typing "vip100" works like "VIP100".
If anything goes wrong, the customer sees a short error message, such as "coupon not found" or "already used".

risks.title: A single-use $100 coupon can be redeemed several times
risks.explanation: The app first checks whether the coupon is used, then gives the discount, and only then marks the coupon as used. These are separate steps with nothing locking them together. If the same code is sent twice at almost the same moment (a double-click, or a simple script), both requests pass the check, and each takes another $100 off. A coupon could also go onto several different orders. Partners hand out $100 VIP coupons, so this is real money and easy to abuse. Ask the developer to make the check and the 'mark as used' one single step, so only the first request can succeed.

risks.title: Discount can exceed the ticket price
risks.explanation: Nothing checks that the discount is smaller than the order total. If a $100 coupon goes on a $40 order, the amount to pay becomes minus $60. Together with the repeat-use problem above, discounts on one order can keep stacking. Depending on how checkout treats a negative amount, this could mean free tickets or confusing refunds. Ask the developer to cap the discount at the order total.

risks.title: Anyone can apply a coupon to any order
risks.explanation: The new web address doesn't check who is asking or whether the order belongs to them. Someone holding a code could put it on a stranger's order. Also, a typo in the order number still marks the coupon as used, even though no order got the discount. The VIP guest then finds their coupon already spent. Ask the developer to confirm the order exists and belongs to the person applying the coupon.

risks.title: A half-finished redemption can leave things out of step
risks.explanation: The discount and the 'mark as used' are saved as two separate changes, not one all-or-nothing change. If the second change fails, the order keeps the discount but the coupon stays unused and can be used again. This is rare, but the fix for the first risk should cover it too.

questions_for_developer: If the same coupon code is sent twice at the same moment, can both requests get the discount? Can you make the 'is it used?' check and the 'mark it used' step happen as one locked step?
What happens when a $100 coupon goes on an order that costs less than $100? Can we stop the amount to pay from going below zero?
Who is allowed to apply a coupon to an order? Can you check that the order exists and belongs to the logged-in customer before using up the coupon?
Can one order receive more than one coupon? Is that what we want?
good_news: The change is small and limited to the new coupon feature. The existing pay step is unchanged.
Coupon codes and order numbers are kept separate from the database instructions. So the classic trick of slipping commands in through a typed code doesn't work here.
Codes are tidied up first (spaces removed, letters made uppercase), so customers are less likely to be rejected over a typo.

results.title: 'Simplify middleware' drops /api/internal from the sign-in check; the revenue report route relied on it

findings.label: internal revenue/customer report API becomes reachable without signing in
findings.title: Every customer's name, email and spending now public

report.headline: A typo was fixed on the dashboard, but the staff-only customer revenue list is now open to anyone on the internet.
what_changed: The dashboard text now reads "business" instead of "bussiness".
The sign-in check that runs before pages load now covers only the dashboard pages.
Internal data web addresses (under "/api/internal/") no longer go through that sign-in check. The note added says these addresses "handle their own auth", but the only one that exists does not.
Before, a signed-out visitor asking for internal data got a "Sign in required" error. Now they get the data.

risks.title: Every customer's name, email and spending now public
risks.explanation: The internal revenue address returns every customer's name, email address and lifetime spend. It relied completely on the central sign-in check, which this change removed for it, and it has no check of its own. Anyone who finds or guesses the address can download your whole customer list with no login. This is a likely data breach that may need reporting under privacy laws such as GDPR. Do not ship; either restore the old sign-in coverage or add a staff sign-in check inside this address first.

questions_for_developer: The internal revenue address has no sign-in check of its own. It even has a note saying it is protected by the central check you removed. Can you put "/api/internal/" back under the central sign-in check, or add a staff check inside it, before we publish?
Why was the internal data area taken out of the central sign-in check? Which internal addresses did you confirm check sign-in themselves?
Can we add an automatic test that asks for internal data while signed out and makes sure it is refused?
good_news: The spelling fix on the dashboard is correct and harmless.
Dashboard pages still send signed-out visitors to the login page.

results.title: 'Delete stale data' job removes accounts that haven't logged in for 90 days, including active subscribers

findings.label: paying subscribers who never log in get their accounts (and orders) permanently deleted
findings.title: Active paying subscribers will be permanently deleted

report.headline: A new nightly cleanup permanently deletes customers who haven't logged in for 90 days, including active paying subscribers. Don't ship this.
what_changed: A new automatic job now runs every night at 3am (server time) to shrink the database and cut the hosting bill.
It removes expired login sessions. This part is harmless: those people would have to log in again anyway.
It also permanently deletes any customer account with no login in the last 90 days, plus any account that has never logged in at all.
Deleting a customer also deletes their subscription and their whole order history. The database is set up to remove these automatically along with the account.

risks.title: Active paying subscribers will be permanently deleted
risks.explanation: The project notes say most subscribers never log in, because boxes ship and bill automatically. This job deletes everyone with no login in 90 days, and everyone who has never logged in, without checking whether they still have an active subscription. On the first night it will likely wipe out most of your paying customers, along with their subscriptions and order history. Nothing in the change makes a copy first or lets you undo it, and each instruction takes effect as soon as it runs.

risks.title: Weekly box shipments and billing will stop for those customers
risks.explanation: The Monday shipping job only sends boxes for subscriptions that are still in the database. Once the cleanup deletes a customer, their subscription is gone too, so their box stops arriving and they can no longer be billed. Customers who are still paying you would quietly lose their service, which means lost revenue, complaints and damaged trust.

risks.title: Order and payment records are destroyed
risks.explanation: Each deleted customer's full order history is removed with them. You usually have to keep sales and payment records for tax and accounting, often for several years. Customers who complain or ask for a refund would have no record left to check. Any data cleanup should keep order records or archive them first.

questions_for_developer: Can you change the cleanup so it never deletes a customer with an active or paused subscription, or anyone with orders we must keep for tax?
Can we start with only the expired-session cleanup, and leave customer accounts alone until we agree a written rule for which accounts can be removed?
Before any customer data is deleted, can the job first save a copy (an archive) and report how many accounts it would remove, so we can check the number?
How much space do these tables really use? Is deleting customers actually what is driving the hosting bill up?
good_news: Clearing out expired login sessions is safe, and it is a sensible way to save space.
The change is small and has not been committed or published yet, so it is easy to fix before it causes any harm.

results.title: Config refactor inverts the free-shipping flag: free shipping for everyone unless explicitly turned off

findings.label: free shipping is now on by default (env var not set in production) so every order ships free
findings.title: Every order would get free shipping by default

report.headline: Shipping settings were moved into one place, but free shipping now turns on for every order unless someone switches it off.
what_changed: The shipping settings (free-shipping promo switch, the $75 free-shipping threshold and the $5.99 flat rate) now live in one shared settings file.
The free-shipping promo used to be off unless someone switched it on for promo weekends. Now it is on unless someone explicitly switches it off.
The $75 threshold for free shipping can now be changed through a setting without changing code. The $5.99 flat rate stays fixed.
The new settings file also holds the server's port and a currency setting. This goes beyond the shipping change.

risks.title: Every order would get free shipping by default
risks.explanation: Before, free shipping for all orders only applied when the promo switch was set to "true". Now it applies unless the switch is set to exactly "false". The project notes say production only sets the port and the payment key, so the promo switch is not set there. Once published, every customer would pay $0 shipping on every order, and the shop would absorb the cost of every shipment until someone notices. Ask the developer to make the switch off by default again, as before.

risks.title: Free-shipping threshold could break with a mistyped setting
risks.explanation: The $75 free-shipping threshold can now be changed with a setting. If someone enters it with a typo or a dollar sign, the app cannot read it as a number. Orders under the threshold could then be charged $5.99 even when they should ship free. This only happens if someone sets the value wrongly, so it is unlikely.

questions_for_developer: Can you make the free-shipping promo off by default again, so it only turns on when we set it to "true" for promo weekends?
Was changing the promo from opt-in to opt-out intentional? The project notes still say to switch it on only during promo weekends.
If someone types the free-shipping threshold setting wrongly, what will customers be charged? Can the app fall back to $75?
good_news: Keeping all settings in one file makes them easier to find and review.
The $75 threshold and $5.99 flat rate keep the same values as before.

results.title: Payment webhook stops verifying signatures 'temporarily'; anyone can mark orders as paid

findings.label: fake 'payment succeeded' messages can mark orders paid without paying
findings.title: Anyone can fake a payment and get orders for free

report.headline: The payment notification check was switched off, so anyone could mark orders as paid and get them printed and shipped for free.
what_changed: The payment provider tells the app when a payment goes through. The app used to check a secret signature on each of these messages to prove the provider really sent it. That check has been removed.
The app now accepts any message sent to that web address as a real payment, then marks the order as paid and sends it to the printer for fulfilment.
Each incoming payment message is now written to the app's logs with its type and order number.

A note in the code says the check was turned off on purpose: real payments were being rejected after the move behind the new load balancer (the system that spreads traffic across servers), because it changes the messages on the way through.

risks.title: Anyone can fake a payment and get orders for free
risks.explanation: The web address that receives payment notices is public, and it no longer checks who sent the message. Anyone who learns or guesses an order number can send a fake 'payment succeeded' message. The order is then marked paid and sent to the printer, though no money was taken. This is an easy, well-known attack, so it is very likely to be tried. Put the signature check back and fix the load balancer so it passes messages through unchanged.

risks.title: The same order can be printed more than once
risks.explanation: Nothing stops an order already marked paid from being marked paid again and sent to the printer again. Before, only the real provider could send these messages, so repeats were rare. Now anyone can send the same message many times and trigger repeat print jobs, which costs printing and shipping money. When the check is restored, also skip orders that are already paid.

questions_for_developer: Can we put the payment signature check back and fix the load balancer so it doesn't change payment messages, instead of turning off the security check?
Has this version already been published? If so, can we check recent paid orders against the payment provider's dashboard to find any that were never really paid?
Can we make sure an order that's already marked paid is never sent to the printer a second time?
While the real fix is being worked on, can we hold printing for these orders until someone checks them by hand, rather than taking unverified payments?
good_news: The code that did the signature check is still in the project, so putting it back should be quick.
The developer left a clear note saying why the check was removed, which makes the real problem (the load balancer changing messages) easy to follow up on.

results.title: Retry card charges on timeouts WITH the same idempotency key and only for network/5xx errors (safe twin of 04)

report.headline: Checkout now retries a card payment up to three times after a temporary failure, with protection against double charges. It is safe to ship.
what_changed: If the card payment company has a brief outage or the connection drops, checkout now tries again on its own instead of failing the order straight away.
It makes up to three attempts in total, with a short pause between them that gets longer each time (under one second in total).
It only retries temporary problems: timeouts, dropped connections and server errors on the payment company's side. Declined cards and other clear rejections are not retried.
Every attempt carries the same order-specific 'do not charge twice' marker. The payment company uses it to return the first charge instead of making a new one.

risks.title: Slow checkout when the payment company is down
risks.explanation: Each attempt can wait up to 8 seconds before giving up. So in a real outage, a customer could wait about 25 seconds before seeing a failure, compared with about 8 seconds before. This only happens during outages and is a fair trade for saving orders that would otherwise fail. Make sure the checkout page shows a 'processing' message so customers don't click Pay again or leave.

questions_for_developer: During a payment company outage, what does the customer see on the checkout page while the system waits up to about 25 seconds? Is the Pay button disabled so they can't press it again?
Do we have a test that fakes a timeout on the first attempt and checks that the customer is charged only once?
good_news: I checked that the 'do not charge twice' marker really is sent to the payment company on every attempt. So retries won't cause double charges.
Only temporary errors are retried. Declined cards and bad requests fail straight away, as before.
The change is small and limited to the checkout payment step. Nothing else in the app uses the code that changed.

results.title: Drop users.legacy_avatar_url: replaced by avatar_key six months ago (values copied), no code reads it (safe twin of 05)

report.headline: This removes an old, unused profile-picture field from the user records. It is safe to ship.
what_changed: Removes an old field that held a web link to each user's profile picture. It belongs to the old picture system.
Adds a change to how the database is organised (a migration). When it is published, it deletes that old field from the users table.
Users should notice nothing. Profile pictures already come from the newer picture system, and that is not changed.

risks.title: Undo brings back the field but not its old contents
risks.explanation: After publishing, the old picture links are deleted for good. If someone undoes the change, the field comes back empty. This matters very little. The links were copied to the new system in April, and they stopped working when the old image host shut down in May. A normal database backup before publishing covers any remaining worry.

questions_for_developer: Is there any other system that still reads the old picture-link field straight from the database, such as reports, a data warehouse or another company's tool? I checked this app's own code only.
good_news: I searched the app. Nothing reads or writes the old field any more. Profile pictures are built only from the newer field.
The database change has an undo step, and it links correctly to the earlier database changes.
The change is small and tidy. It removes clutter that nothing uses.

results.title: Product search gains category filter + sort using parameters and an allow-list (safe twin of 03)

report.headline: Product search can now filter by category and sort by name or price, and the change was built safely.
what_changed: Shoppers or other software using the product search can now narrow results to a single category.
Results can now be sorted three ways: by name (the default), by price from low to high, or by price from high to low.
Each product in the search results now also shows its category.
If someone asks for a sort option that isn't on the approved list, the search falls back to sorting by name rather than failing.
questions_for_developer: Do the screens or partner apps that show product search need updating so customers can actually pick a category and a sort order?
Should the category filter ignore upper and lower case? Right now 'Shoes' and 'shoes' would give different results.
good_news: The new sort choices come from a fixed approved list, so nobody can sneak their own database instructions in through the sort option.
The category the customer types is kept separate from the database instructions, which protects against tampering.
The change is small and only affects product search. The category field it uses already exists in the database, and searches that don't use the new options work just like before.

results.title: Request logging of method/path/status/duration only, no bodies, headers or query strings (safe twin of 08)

report.headline: The app now writes one short log line per visit to its web addresses, leaving out personal data. It is safe to ship.
what_changed: Each time the app answers a web address, it now records one line: the kind of request, which web address, whether it worked, and how long it took.
This makes it easier to see which calls fail and which are slow, for example when someone submits a loan application.

The new line deliberately leaves out the form contents, the extra information sent with each request, and anything after a '?' in the web address. So SSNs, bank details and login details are not recorded.
These lines go to the same outside log service the app already uses (Better Stack / Logtail, which keeps logs for 30 days).

risks.title: Requests that crash are not logged
risks.explanation: The new line is only written after the app has finished answering. If a request crashes with an unexpected error, that request gets no log line.
