So the most serious failures can be missing from this new view. Your error monitoring may still catch them, but a developer could easily add a log line for crashes too.

risks.title: More log lines sent to the paid log service
risks.explanation: Every request now sends one extra line to the outside log service, so log volume grows with traffic. Each line is tiny and is sent in the background, so customers won't see any slowdown. If your log plan charges by volume, keep an eye on the bill.

questions_for_developer: Can we also log a line when a request crashes with an unexpected error, so the worst failures show up in the same place?
Will any future web address include personal details in the address itself (for example a customer ID or email)? The new log records the full address, minus anything after a '?'.
good_news: The developer kept personal data out on purpose. Today the loan application address contains no personal details, so nothing sensitive ends up in the outside log service.
The change is small and self-contained, and it doesn't change how loan applications are handled.
Logs are sent in the background, so this won't slow down pages for customers.

results.title: Shop checkout: promo + referral codes can stack without limit

findings.label: discount codes stack (same code twice / total can reach zero or below)
findings.title: Discounts can be repeated without limit

report.headline: Checkout now allows promo combinations, but it also lets customers reuse every code without limits.
what_changed: Customers can apply more than one discount code at checkout.
The checkout total now adds the discount from each applied code.
A test was added for combining a referral offer with a seasonal offer.

risks.title: Discounts can be repeated without limit
risks.explanation: A customer can submit the same valid code repeatedly, and each use reduces the order again. They can also combine every valid code, rather than only one referral code and one seasonal offer. This can reduce an order to zero or below its price, so do not ship until checkout rejects repeated codes and enforces the intended combination rules.

good_news: The added test confirms the intended referral-plus-seasonal combination.

results.title: Signup stores passwords in plain text after removing the hashing library

findings.label: passwords stored/compared in plain text
findings.title: Passwords are stored in readable form

report.headline: The new password reminder exposes passwords and stops existing customers from signing in.
what_changed: Customers can now request an email that claims to remind them of their password.
New customer passwords are kept in readable form instead of protected form.
Existing customer sign-ins will no longer work after this change.

risks.title: Passwords are stored in readable form
risks.explanation: Anyone who gains access to the customer database can read every new password. People often reuse passwords, so this can expose accounts beyond this product. Restore one-way password protection before publishing.

risks.title: Existing customers cannot sign in
risks.explanation: Passwords saved before this change were stored in a protected scrambled form. The new sign-in check only accepts a readable stored password, so those customers will be rejected. Keep support for the existing protected form, then safely update it after successful sign-in.

risks.title: Password emails expose customer secrets
risks.explanation: For newly created accounts, the password reminder sends the actual password by email. Anyone who accesses a customer's mailbox or a copied email can take over the account. Send a short-lived, single-use reset link instead.

questions_for_developer: Can you replace the password reminder with a short-lived, single-use reset link and restore protected password storage?
How will existing customers keep signing in after the password storage change?
good_news: The password reminder avoids confirming whether an email address has an account.

results.title: Product search builds SQL from user input (SQL injection)

findings.label: SQL injection in product search/sort
findings.title: Visitors can alter the database

report.headline: The new product search allows visitors to run harmful database instructions, so it should not ship yet.
what_changed: Product search can now narrow results by category and sort results.
Search results now include each product's category.
When a search fails, the app sends the full database instruction back to the visitor.

risks.title: Visitors can alter the database
risks.explanation: Search text, category, and sorting choices are placed directly into database instructions. Anyone who can reach product search can send crafted values that change those instructions. Depending on the database account's permissions, they could read data they should not see, change product records, or delete them. Keep visitor values separate from database instructions, and only allow a fixed list of sorting choices.

risks.title: Database details leak on errors
risks.explanation: If a search fails, the response includes both the error and the full database instruction. This gives an attacker useful details about the data structure and makes the first issue easier to exploit. Return a general error to visitors and keep detailed failure information only in protected staff logs.

good_news: The change is limited to the product-search web address.

results.title: Checkout retries card charges without an idempotency key (double charge)

findings.label: retrying a charge can bill the customer twice
findings.title: Customers can be charged repeatedly

report.headline: The checkout retry removes double-charge protection, so customers can be charged more than once.
what_changed: The checkout page now retries a payment up to four times after an error.
The payment request no longer includes protection against doing the same charge twice.
Each retry uses a different time-stamped payment description.

risks.title: Customers can be charged repeatedly
risks.explanation: A timeout can happen after the payment company has accepted a charge but before the app receives its reply. The new retry then sends another charge without protection against doing the same thing twice, up to four times. This can create duplicate charges, refunds, support work, and lost customer trust. Restore the stable order-based duplicate-charge protection on every retry, and keep the payment description stable.

results.title: Migration drops users.phone while SMS reminders still read it

findings.label: dropping phone column deletes data and breaks SMS reminders that still use it
findings.title: Release cannot be safely undone

report.headline: This removes customer phone numbers, but the database change cannot be undone safely after publishing.
what_changed: Customer phone numbers will be removed from the product database.
The app will no longer keep a phone number on each user record.
The change says phone contacts have moved to the new customer system.

risks.title: Release cannot be safely undone
risks.explanation: The change removes the phone-number column but provides no undo action. If publishing causes a problem and the team restores the earlier app version, that version may fail because it still expects phone numbers to exist. Ask the developer to add an undo path before publishing, or confirm that restoring the earlier version is impossible by design.

questions_for_developer: Have all existing phone numbers been copied to the new customer system and checked before they are permanently removed?
good_news: The removal is small and limited to the customer phone-number field.

results.title: Live payment secret key hard-coded and .env.production committed

findings.label: live secret key committed to the code
findings.title: Live payment secret exposed

report.headline: The change exposes a live payment secret and can send preview payments to the real account.
what_changed: Production payment settings were added to the repository.
Preview versions of the checkout can now use the company’s live payment account when their payment setting is missing.
The repository no longer protects environment setting files from being added.

risks.title: Live payment secret exposed
risks.explanation: A live payment secret appears in both a tracked settings file and the application source. Anyone who receives this code or its history could use the company’s payment account, including accessing payment-related customer information or creating payment actions. Do not publish this change; revoke and replace the exposed secret, remove it from the repository history, and store it only in the hosting provider’s private settings.

risks.title: Preview checkout uses live payments
risks.explanation: When a preview version lacks its payment setting, checkout silently uses the live payment account. A tester or preview visitor could create real charges instead of a safe test payment. Keep previews disabled when the setting is missing, or give them a separate test payment account.

risks.title: Future settings can be committed
risks.explanation: The change removes the rule that excluded environment setting files from the repository. This makes it easy to accidentally publish future secrets, such as payment, email, or database access details. Restore the protection and keep only a secret-free example settings file in the repository.

questions_for_developer: Has the exposed live payment secret already been revoked and replaced in the payment provider and hosting settings?

results.title: New admin API route (delete user / change role) has no admin check

findings.label: admin delete/role-change route reachable without being an admin
findings.title: Anyone may control user accounts

report.headline: The admin user screen can now change roles and permanently delete users without visible access controls.
what_changed: The user-management screen now lets staff change a person's role.
The screen now lets staff delete a person after a confirmation message.
The app now accepts requests to change roles or delete users at a new web address.

risks.title: Anyone may control user accounts
risks.explanation: The new web address changes roles and deletes accounts, but it contains no check that the caller is signed in or is an administrator. A person could send requests to it directly, without using the admin screen. They could make themselves an administrator or delete other users, causing loss of access and user data. Add and verify a server-side administrator check before either action.

questions_for_developer: Is there a site-wide access rule that protects this new web address, including direct requests from people who do not use the admin screen? Please show where it is enforced.
When a user is deleted, does the database reliably delete their shifts as the confirmation message promises, or could the deletion fail because shifts still exist?
good_news: The confirmation message reduces accidental deletions from the admin screen.

results.title: Debug middleware logs full request bodies (SSN, card numbers) to a third-party log service

findings.label: personal/payment data written to logs (shipped to log provider)
findings.title: Customer details enter logs

report.headline: This change records every customer request in full, creating a serious privacy and security risk.
what_changed: The app now records details for every visit and form submission.
The records include each visitor’s extra request information and the full text they submitted.
The records also include whether the app accepted or rejected each request and how long it took.

risks.title: Customer details enter logs
risks.explanation: Every submitted form is copied into the app’s records. For a lending product, this can include applicants’ contact, financial, and other sensitive details. Anyone with access to these records could see that data, and keeping it there increases the damage from an account breach. Remove or mask personal details before recording requests.

risks.title: Login secrets enter logs
risks.explanation: The change copies all extra request information into the records. That can include login proof, browser session identifiers, or other access secrets sent by customers. A person who can read the records could use such secrets to access customer accounts while they remain valid. Never record these values; remove sensitive entries before logging.

good_news: The change is small and can be made safe by recording only the request type, web address, result, and timing.

results.title: Ticket-summary job re-summarises every ticket every minute with unbounded retries/recursion

findings.label: AI bill can blow up (every ticket every minute, unlimited retries/recursion)
findings.title: AI spending can grow without limit

report.headline: The new inbox summaries send every support ticket to a paid AI service every minute, creating uncontrolled cost and privacy exposure.
what_changed: The inbox can now show short summaries of support conversations.
Every existing support ticket is re-summarized once per minute, not only when its conversation changes.
Each support conversation is sent to an outside AI provider to create its preview.

risks.title: AI spending can grow without limit
risks.explanation: Every minute, the change sends every ticket to a paid AI service. As ticket history grows, costs grow continuously even when no customer has written anything new. Failed requests retry forever, and long summaries trigger extra requests, so an outage or unexpected response can increase spending further. Do not ship until this runs only for changed tickets and has firm spending, retry, and concurrency limits.

risks.title: All support conversations leave the company
risks.explanation: The change sends the full text of every support conversation to an outside AI provider once per minute. Support messages can contain names, contact details, account information, or sensitive complaints. Confirm this sharing is covered by the company’s privacy commitments and provider agreement, and limit or remove sensitive information before sending it.

risks.title: Repeated jobs may pile up
risks.explanation: A new run starts every minute even if the previous run is still processing many tickets. Each run starts work for every ticket at once, which can overload the database or AI provider and make summaries fall behind. Prevent overlapping runs and process a controlled number of tickets at a time.

questions_for_developer: What limit will stop AI spending if requests fail, responses remain too long, or ticket volume rises?
Can we summarize only tickets that changed since their last summary, instead of every ticket every minute?
Has the company approved sending all support conversations, including possible personal information, to this AI provider?
good_news: The database update keeps each summary linked to its correct ticket.

results.title: Renewals moved to customer-local midnight; mixed time zones cause double/missed charges

findings.label: time-zone mix-up bills some customers twice (and skips day-31 renewals)
findings.title: Some customers can be charged twice

report.headline: The new local-date billing logic can double-charge some customers and skip others’ monthly charges.
what_changed: Renewals now use each customer’s local calendar day.
The protection against repeat charges now changes every hour.
The next scheduled renewal date is no longer saved after charging.

risks.title: Some customers can be charged twice
risks.explanation: A customer’s renewal day is checked in their time zone, but the record of their last charge uses the server’s calendar day. Around midnight, these dates can differ. If the renewal job runs again, a customer can be charged twice on the same local renewal day; the repeat-charge protection also changes each hour, so it will not stop a later attempt. Do not ship until both dates and the repeat-charge protection use the same customer-local renewal date.

risks.title: Short months can skip renewals
risks.explanation: The new rule only charges when the calendar has the exact saved day number. Customers billed on the 29th, 30th, or 31st will not be charged in months that lack that day, such as February. The previous approach calculated the next renewal date, so confirm and restore the intended handling for shorter months before publishing.

questions_for_developer: When a month lacks a customer’s saved renewal day, should we charge on its last day or use another rule?
Does the renewal job run more than once per day? If so, can you make the stored billing date and repeat-charge protection use the customer’s local date?
good_news: The change still limits renewals to active subscriptions.

results.title: Marketing copy edits and typo fixes

report.headline: The update fixes copy errors and makes trial wording clearer across the home and pricing pages.
what_changed: The home page now fixes spelling errors and describes searching scanned pages more clearly.
Calls to action now say “Start your free trial” on the home and pricing pages.
The pricing page fixes spelling and clarifies that the free trial lasts 14 days.
good_news: This is a small, contained wording-only change with no effect on prices, payments, customer data, or sign-up links.

results.title: Refactor: extract duplicated money formatting into a helper (no behaviour change)

report.headline: Invoice prices now use one shared display rule, with no verified customer-facing problem.
what_changed: Invoice line items and invoice totals now show prices through the same shared formatting rule.
Dollar, euro, and pound amounts keep their symbols, while other currencies show their currency code.
New checks confirm comma separators, cents, and an unsupported currency display correctly.
questions_for_developer: Is the individual invoice-line display helper used anywhere outside this invoice module? Its calling pattern changed, so any outside use must be updated.
good_news: The total calculation remains the same, so this change does not alter what customers are charged.
The price-display logic is now kept in one place, reducing the chance that invoice lines and totals show different amounts.

results.title: Add a /healthz endpoint for the load balancer

report.headline: The app now offers a simple health check web address with its current version, and the change is safe to ship.
what_changed: Load balancers can check whether the app is running through a new health check web address.
The health check returns a successful result and the app version.
The project notes now list the parcel lookup and health check web addresses.
A new automated check confirms the health check response.
good_news: The new behavior is small and separate from parcel tracking.
The health check does not expose customer or parcel information.

results.title: Add a dark-mode toggle (preference saved in the browser)

report.headline: The recipe search screen now offers a saved light or dark display mode and is safe to ship.
what_changed: Customers can switch the Recipe Box screen between light and dark display modes.
The app remembers each customer’s choice on their device.
New visitors start with the display mode their device prefers.

risks.title: Brief light-mode flash
risks.explanation: Customers who prefer dark mode may briefly see the light screen when the page first opens. This is most noticeable on slower devices and does not affect recipes or searches. A developer can avoid it by applying the saved choice before the page first appears.

good_news: The choice is stored only on the customer’s own device and is not sent to a company service.
The change is small and does not alter recipe search or recipe data.

results.title: Add 'download my invoices as CSV' (properly scoped to the signed-in customer)

report.headline: Customers can download their own invoices as a CSV spreadsheet, with account checks preserved.
what_changed: Customers can download their invoice list as an accountant-friendly CSV file.
The download includes invoice number, issue date, total, and payment status.
The existing invoice list now uses the same customer-only selection rule as the download.
good_news: The export limits results to the signed-in customer, so it does not expose other customers’ invoices.
The file download has a fixed filename and is limited to the customer’s existing invoice data.

results.title: Partial refunds from support dashboard: remaining-balance check dropped (buried in a mixed diff)

findings.label: support can refund more than the customer paid / refund the same order repeatedly
findings.title: Refunds can exceed the remaining balance

report.headline: Partial refunds can overpay customers or be sent twice, so this should not ship yet.
what_changed: Support staff can now enter a refund amount or leave it empty to refund the remaining balance.
The refund screen uses shorter labels and clearer customer-facing timing.
Refund records now show the dollar amount in staff logs.
The README now says that partial refunds are supported.

risks.title: Refunds can exceed the remaining balance
risks.explanation: The new partial-refund path sends any entered amount without checking it is positive or no more than the unpaid refund balance. A staff member can enter more than remains, including after an earlier partial refund. This can overpay a customer if the payment service accepts the request. Check the amount before sending it, and reject amounts above the remaining balance.

risks.title: A retry can send a second refund
risks.explanation: Each refund attempt now gets a new unique label based on the current time. If the payment succeeds but saving the order fails, a retry looks like a new request. For a partial refund, the payment service can then send the same refund again, while the order may record only one. Keep one stable protection label for a given refund attempt and save a durable refund record.

good_news: The customer-facing refund timing now says business days, which is clearer.
The change is limited to refunds, wording, and documentation.

results.title: New invoice PDF download checks login but not ownership (any customer can read any invoice)

findings.label: any signed-in customer can download other customers' invoices by changing the number
findings.title: Customers can access others’ invoices

report.headline: Invoice downloads expose any customer’s invoice details to other signed-in customers.
what_changed: Customers can now download invoice documents from their invoice list.
The invoice list now includes each invoice’s internal reference number for use in downloads.

risks.title: Customers can access others’ invoices
risks.explanation: The new invoice download address only checks that someone is signed in. It does not check that the requested invoice belongs to that person. A signed-in customer could change the invoice number in the web address and download another customer’s invoice, including their email address and billed total. Block release until the download confirms ownership before creating the file.

risks.title: Downloaded PDFs may not display
risks.explanation: The generated document asks the PDF viewer to use a font that the document never defines. It also places invoice text into the document without handling characters that have special meaning in PDFs. Customers may receive blank or broken invoices, especially when invoice or customer details contain unusual characters. Use a tested PDF generator, or create a complete valid document and test representative invoices.

good_news: The invoice list remains limited to the signed-in customer.
The change does not alter invoice totals or payment records.

results.title: Refactor payment client into a module with typed errors (behaviour and double-charge protection unchanged)

report.headline: Checkout payments behave the same, with clearer payment-failure details for future handling.
what_changed: Customers still receive the same checkout charge, order status, description, and protection against duplicate charges.
Payment failures now carry the payment service’s response code, which can support clearer handling later.
good_news: The change is small and preserves the existing checkout payment details and duplicate-charge protection.
No customer data, payment amount, or payment destination changed.

results.title: Add an optional 'marketing emails' preference column (off by default) with a safe migration

report.headline: The app adds an optional newsletter choice that starts turned off for every patient.
what_changed: Patients can choose whether they want the clinic newsletter from their profile.
Existing and new patient records start with newsletter messages turned off.
The database is updated to save each patient's newsletter choice.

risks.title: Undoing release loses choices
risks.explanation: If the team publishes this change, patients set their choices, and then undoes the release, the database change removes those saved choices. This only affects a rollback, but it would lose newly collected preference data. Export those choices before undoing the release, if a rollback becomes necessary.

questions_for_developer: Where will the newsletter-sending process check this new choice before sending an email, and will it also honor any existing unsubscribe records?
How does the profile screen ensure a patient can change only their own newsletter choice?
good_news: Newsletter messages are off by default, including for existing patients.
The change is small and does not alter appointments, payments, or contact details.

results.title: Big diff (vendored 400 KB chart library) hides a public, unauthenticated customer export

findings.label: customer export (emails, phones, spend) downloadable by anyone without signing in
findings.title: Customer list is public

report.headline: The new public reports expose every customer’s personal details without requiring a staff login.
what_changed: The home page now shows a customer-list download link and loads chart add-on code.
Anyone who knows the report web addresses can request monthly order totals.
Anyone can download a customer list containing names, email addresses, phone numbers, birthdays, and lifetime spending.

risks.title: Customer list is public

risks.title: Removed safety rule makes future secret leaks easier

questions_for_developer: Has the live payment secret key already been pushed to a shared repository? If yes, has it been cancelled in the payment dashboard and replaced?
Why do preview versions of the site not have the payment setting? Can a test-mode key be added to the hosting settings for previews instead?
Can the fallback to the live key be removed, so the site stops with a clear error when the setting is missing rather than charging real cards?
Can the settings file be removed from this change and the old sharing rule restored?
good_news: The change touches only three files, so reverting it is quick and simple.
The live publishable key is meant to be visible in the website, so that part is less serious than the secret key.

results.title: New admin API route (delete user / change role) has no admin check

findings.label: admin delete/role-change route reachable without being an admin
findings.title: Anyone can change any user's role, including making themselves admin

report.headline: Adds buttons to the admin users page to change roles and delete users, but the new actions have no admin check.
what_changed: The admin users screen now has a role dropdown (member, manager, admin) for each person.
The admin users screen now has a Delete button for each person. It asks for confirmation first, and deleting also removes that person's shifts.
The role dropdown and Delete button send their requests to a new web address the app answers. That address skips the admin check that the existing user list uses.
Nothing else in the app was changed.

risks.title: Anyone can change any user's role, including making themselves admin
risks.explanation: The new role-change address does not check whether the person asking is an admin. The existing user list does check, so this new part was missed. The sign-in check on the admin pages only runs when someone opens a page. It does not protect this address. Someone who is not an admin could send a request that makes their own account admin, and then manage everyone. Likelihood is high, since the address is reachable by anyone who knows it. Fix by adding the same admin check used on the user list to both new actions before shipping.

risks.title: Anyone can delete any user and all their shift records, with no undo
risks.explanation: The new delete address has the same missing admin check. Anyone who can reach it could delete staff accounts. Deleting an account also deletes all of that person's shifts, which the database is set up to do automatically. There is no backup step or recycle bin in this change, so the data cannot be recovered from the app. This could affect pay records and schedules. Fix by adding the admin check, and confirm that backups exist and that shift history should really be removed with the account.

risks.title: Role value is not checked, so any text can be saved as a role
risks.explanation: The dropdown only offers three roles, but the server accepts whatever text it is sent. A bad or mistyped role could be saved. The app may then treat that person as having no access, or in a way no one expects. Likelihood is low for normal use, but it is easy to avoid. Fix by allowing only member, manager and admin on the server.

questions_for_developer: Can you add the same admin check that the user list uses to the role-change and delete actions, and test that a non-admin gets refused?
Should deleting a person also delete their shift history, or should we keep shifts for pay and records and only remove the account?
Can the server accept only the three allowed roles, and reject anything else?
Do we have recent database backups, and is there a way to restore a deleted user if this is shipped by mistake?

The delete button asks the person to confirm before anything is removed.
The existing user list already checks for an admin, so the correct pattern is already in the codebase to copy.

results.title: Debug middleware logs full request bodies (SSN, card numbers) to a third-party log service

findings.title: Applicants' SSNs and bank details sent to a third-party log service

report.headline: This change records every web request in full, including applicants' SSNs and bank account numbers, and sends them to an outside log service.
what_changed: Every request the app receives is now written to the logs, with its full contents and its sender's login details.

The app's logs go to Logtail, an outside log search service that keeps them for 30 days, so this sensitive information would leave your systems.
The change is small: two new lines plus one new file. It was made to help debug the failed applications problem.

risks.title: Applicants' SSNs and bank details sent to a third-party log service
risks.explanation: Each loan application's full contents, including Social Security number, date of birth, bank account number and routing number, would be written to the logs. The app's existing setup sends every log entry to Logtail, an outside service that keeps them for 30 days. Every applicant would be affected, starting with the next application submitted. This likely breaks privacy promises to applicants and may breach data protection rules and contracts. Remove the full-body logging before release, and check whether any sensitive data has already reached Logtail.

risks.title: Login details written to logs
risks.explanation: The change logs every request's headers. These can include login tokens and session cookies. risks.title: Application submissions may hang or arrive empty
risks.explanation: The new code reads the full request body before passing it on to the application form handler. In this FastAPI and Starlette setup, that can leave the handler with an empty or stalled body. If so, customers submitting loan applications could see failures, which matches the failed-applications problem this was meant to debug. This is unverified because no test was run. Test one submission on a staging copy before release.

questions_for_developer: Can the request logging be limited to the method, the web address, the status code and the time taken, with no body and no headers?
Has anyone checked what has already been sent to Logtail since this code was added? If it has not run in production yet, can we confirm that?
Does our Logtail contract allow storing Social Security numbers and bank details? If not, which logs must be cleaned up?
Can you submit a test loan application on a staging copy and confirm the handler still receives the full form data?

results.title: Ticket-summary job re-summarises every ticket every minute with unbounded retries/recursion

findings.label: AI bill can blow up (every ticket every minute, unlimited retries/recursion)
findings.title: Paid AI calls for every ticket, every minute

report.headline: The change adds an AI job that re-summarizes every support ticket every minute, which could run up large bills.
what_changed: Every minute, the system will ask an outside AI service (OpenAI) to write a three-sentence summary of every support ticket.
The summaries are saved on each ticket and shown as short previews in the inbox.
Tickets are re-summarized on every run, even when nothing has changed since the last one.
Each ticket's full conversation text is sent to the AI company each time.
The existing nightly job that closes stale tickets is not changed.

risks.title: Paid AI calls for every ticket, every minute
risks.explanation: The job runs every minute and sends every ticket to the paid AI service on each run, with no check for new or changed tickets and no daily limit. That is about 1,440 runs a day, so 1,000 tickets would mean roughly 1.4 million paid requests a day. Bills could grow quickly, and runs can pile up if one run is still going when the next starts. Fix: summarize a ticket only when it gets a new message, run far less often, and set a spending limit with the AI provider.

risks.title: Endless retries and no limit when the AI service fails
risks.explanation: If the AI service is down, the key is wrong, or the account runs out of credit, the code retries forever with no pause, and every retry can still be billed. Summaries longer than 280 characters are also sent back for another summary with no limit on how many times. All tickets are sent at once, which can trigger the provider's rate limits and cause more failures. Fix: cap the retries, add a pause between them, and limit how many requests run at the same time.

risks.title: Full customer conversations sent to an outside AI company
risks.explanation: Every ticket's complete message history is sent to OpenAI every minute. Customers may not expect their support conversations to go to a third-party AI company, and this may not match the privacy policy or the terms with the provider. Before shipping, confirm that the privacy policy allows this and that the contract covers this use. Consider sending only what is needed for a short summary.

questions_for_developer: How many support tickets exist today, and how many new messages arrive each day? Please estimate the monthly AI bill for this job before it goes live.
Can the summary be created once per ticket and redone only when a new message arrives, instead of every minute?
What happens when the AI service is down or out of credit? Can the job stop after a few tries and wait before trying again?

Does the tickets table already have a summary column? If not, the save step will fail on every run. Also, does our privacy policy and contract with OpenAI allow sending customer conversations to them?
good_news: The change is small: two files and 37 added lines, which makes it easy to review and to undo.
The job only writes a summary field. It does not email customers or change ticket status.
The existing nightly ticket-closing job is left alone.

results.title: Renewals moved to customer-local midnight; mixed time zones cause double/missed charges

findings.label: time-zone mix-up bills some customers twice (and skips day-31 renewals)
findings.title: Customers can be charged twice on the same renewal day

report.headline: The change bills customers on their own local day, but it can charge the same customer twice and skips renewals on days 29 to 31.
what_changed: Customers are now billed on their renewal day in their own time zone, instead of at the exact signup time.
The billing job checks every hour whether a customer's renewal day has started in that customer's time zone.
Each charge now carries a duplicate-protection reference that changes every hour, instead of one fixed reference per renewal date. This was not asked for in the description.
The stored next renewal time is no longer moved forward after a charge. The billing date is now recorded as the day the charge ran.
Customers who signed up on the 29th, 30th or 31st will not be charged in months that do not have that day. The old code moved their charge to the last day of the month.

risks.title: Customers can be charged twice on the same renewal day
risks.explanation: The job compares the customer's local date with the billing computer's date, but records the billing date using the computer's date. Assuming the computer runs on UTC, almost every customer outside UTC is affected. For example, a Los Angeles customer is charged just after local midnight, then charged again later that day when the computer's date changes, because the recorded date does not match. The hourly reference changes too, so the payment company will not block the second charge. Fix before shipping: use the customer's time zone for both the check and the recorded date, and test with a non-UTC customer.

risks.title: Customers signed up on days 29 to 31 are skipped in short months
risks.explanation: The new check only bills when today's day number matches the renewal day exactly. A customer signed up on the 31st will never match in months with 30 days or fewer, so that month's payment is never collected. The old code handled this by moving the charge to the last day of the month, and that helper still exists in the code but is no longer used. Fix before shipping: restore the last-day fallback for short months.

risks.title: A retry after a failed or slow charge can charge the customer again
risks.explanation: The old reference stayed the same for the whole renewal date, so the payment company could recognise a repeat. The new reference includes the current hour, so a retry in a later hour looks like a new payment. If the first charge went through but the reply timed out (the code waits 15 seconds), the next hourly run charges again. Fix before shipping: keep the reference fixed per customer per renewal date.

questions_for_developer: Does the billing job save the 'last billed' date to the database right after each charge? The save step in the repository is only a placeholder, so this cannot be confirmed from here.
Should every customer get one fixed charge reference per renewal date, so a retry can never charge twice?
For customers signed up on the 29th to 31st, should the charge fall on the last day of short months, as the old code did?
Does anything outside this repository, such as the app or customer emails, show the old 'next billing date'? That field is no longer updated, so it could show wrong dates.
What happens if a customer's time zone is missing or invalid? Would that stop the whole hourly run before other customers are billed?
good_news: The change is small and limited to one file, which makes the fixes easy to target.
The code still records the charge after the payment succeeds, so a failed payment is not marked as billed.
The duplicate-protection header is still sent to the payment company, so fixing the reference is enough to restore that protection.

results.title: Add a /healthz endpoint for the load balancer

Should the health check also confirm that parcel lookups work, or is a simple 'server is running' check enough for the load balancer?

results.title: Add a dark-mode toggle (preference saved in the browser)

results.title: Add 'download my invoices as CSV' (properly scoped to the signed-in customer)

results.title: Partial refunds from support dashboard: remaining-balance check dropped (buried in a mixed diff)

findings.label: support can refund more than the customer paid / refund the same order repeatedly

report.headline: Partial refunds were added, but the new code can refund too much and can pay the same refund twice.
what_changed: Support agents can now refund part of a member's order, such as one missed class, by typing an amount.
If the amount is left empty, the refund covers whatever is still unrefunded on the order, as before.
The refund button now says "Refund", and a new field asks for the amount to refund.

risks.title: Repeated clicks or retries can refund the member twice
risks.explanation: Each refund request now gets a new, unique reference based on the current time. The payment company uses that reference to spot a repeated request, so with a new reference every repeat goes through as a new refund. A double click, a slow connection, or two agents acting at once could each pay out money. The old version used a fixed reference for full refunds, which blocked this.

risks.title: Refund amount is not checked against what was paid
risks.explanation: The typed amount is never compared with the amount paid or the amount already refunded. A typing mistake, such as 200 instead of 20, would refund 200. Removing the old check also means a refund on a fully refunded order now sends a zero or negative amount to the payment company instead of stopping. Those requests may be rejected, or they may be misread by the payment system.

questions_for_developer: Where is the refund button connected to this code, and does that screen check the typed amount before it sends the refund?
Can each refund request carry a stable reference, so that a repeated click or retry cannot pay out the same money twice?
Should the code block any refund larger than the amount still unrefunded, and block refunds on orders that are already fully refunded, as the old version did?

report.headline: This change emails a 40% discount to inactive users after every publish, including people who unsubscribed.
what_changed: Every time the app is published, a win-back email offering 40% off is sent to inactive users.
A user counts as inactive if they have not been active for 30 days, or have never been active.
The email uses the subject "We miss you! 40% off your next course" and the discount code COMEBACK40.
The send runs as an extra step after the normal publish step. If it fails, the publish is reported as failed.
No screens, payments or existing customer features were changed.

risks.title: Emails go to people who already unsubscribed
risks.explanation: The customer list records when someone unsubscribes, but the new send step never checks that record. People who asked to stop getting emails will receive a marketing offer anyway. This breaks anti-spam and privacy rules such as CAN-SPAM (US) and GDPR (EU), and can lead to complaints and fines. Fix: skip every user who has an unsubscribe date before sending.

risks.title: Same customers get the offer again on every publish
risks.explanation: The send step is attached to the after-publish command, so it runs each time the app is published. It keeps no record of who was already emailed, so inactive users can get the 40% offer again and again, sometimes within days. Fix: record each send and skip anyone already emailed, or remove this step from the publish command and run it once on purpose.

risks.title: Marketing email has no unsubscribe link or company address
risks.explanation: The email body contains only a greeting and the discount code. It has no unsubscribe link and no postal address, which marketing emails normally need under anti-spam laws. Customers who want out have no simple way to opt out from this email.

risks.title: One failed email stops the run and causes repeats
risks.explanation: The loop has no error handling. If the mail service rejects one email, the whole run stops, the publish step fails, and a retry would send emails again to the people who were already reached. This is a realistic outcome given that mail services sometimes fail.

questions_for_developer: Can you make the send skip every user who has an unsubscribe date, and confirm that before it sends?
Can you stop this email from being sent on every publish, so each customer gets it only once, and record who has been sent it?
Is the code COMEBACK40 real, limited to one use per customer, and set to expire? Who approved a 40% discount for this list?
Should people who have never used the app (no activity date at all) get a discount email? Do we have their consent to email them?
Can you add an unsubscribe link and our company postal address to the email, as anti-spam laws require?
good_news: The change is small and contained, touching only two files.
The mail sending key is kept in a setting rather than written into the code.
The customer list already has an unsubscribe field, so the fix is simple to make.

results.title: Gift-card purchase passes a dollar amount where the gateway expects cents (charges 100x too little)

findings.label: gift cards charged in dollars as if cents: a $50 card costs 50 cents
findings.title: Gift cards would charge one hundredth of their price

report.headline: The new gift card purchase would charge customers one hundredth of the price, so it should not ship yet.
what_changed: Adds a gift card purchase feature in the code. No screen or customer page uses it yet, so no one has been charged.
Gift cards are offered at $25, $50 and $100.
Each purchase charges the buyer and creates a random 16-character code meant to be given to the recipient.
The project's README gets a short note describing the gift card purchase.

risks.title: Gift cards would charge one hundredth of their price
risks.explanation: Gift card prices are stored in dollars, but the payment step reads the number as cents. A $25 card would charge 25 cents, and a $100 card would charge $1. Nothing calls the feature yet, so no customer has been charged. If it goes live as written, the business would collect a tiny fraction of each sale, and receipts would not match what customers saw. The fix is to convert dollars to cents before charging, and to add a test that checks the amount.

risks.title: Gift card codes are never saved, so buyers may pay for nothing
risks.explanation: The purchase step creates the code and hands it back, but nothing stores it. No redemption step exists in this project either, so a code could not be used even if the buyer received it. If the feature went live without that work, customers would pay for a card they could not use. Save each code with its purchase record before the charge is made, and build redemption before launch.

risks.title: A timed-out payment could charge a buyer with no code issued
risks.explanation: The payment call gives up after 8 seconds. If the card is charged but the reply is lost, the purchase fails and the new code is thrown away, leaving a charge with no record to match it to. The duplicate-charge safeguard uses a code generated fresh on each attempt, so a manual retry would not be blocked and could charge the buyer twice. Use a stored purchase record and a stable reference per purchase, and check the gateway before retrying.

questions_for_developer: Is the gift card price in the catalog meant to be dollars? Please confirm that a $25 card sends 2,500 to the payment service, and fix the conversion before launch.
Where will each gift card code be stored, and how will a customer redeem it at checkout? Is redemption built anywhere else?
If a payment times out after the card was charged, how will we find that charge and give the buyer their code? Should we save a purchase record before charging?
Will the recipient get an email with the code? If so, does the email check the address and respect people who have opted out of emails?
good_news: Nothing customer-facing uses the feature yet, so no customer has been charged wrongly.
The change is small and contained: two new files and a short note in the README.
The existing payment code already expects amounts in cents, so the fix is one contained conversion.

results.title: Single-use coupon checked then marked used in separate steps (can be redeemed many times in parallel)

findings.label: the same single-use coupon can be redeemed several times by simultaneous requests
findings.title: Same $100 coupon can be used twice at the same moment

report.headline: Adds a coupon field to orders, but the single-use check can be beaten by two requests at once.
what_changed: Customers can now type a coupon code into their order, and the discount is added to the order total.
Each coupon is meant to work once. Partner coupons are worth $100 off and are given to VIP guests.
The code trims spaces and turns the coupon code into capitals before checking it.
A missing or unknown code, or a code already used, gives the customer a short error message.
No emails, texts or customer messages are sent by this change.

risks.title: Same $100 coupon can be used twice at the same moment
risks.explanation: The system first checks whether the coupon is unused, then marks it used in a separate step. If two requests with the same code arrive at nearly the same time, both can pass the check before either marks it used. The same guest could then get the $100 off twice, or a guest could share a code and have several people use it. Partner coupons are meant to be single-use, so this is lost revenue. It is most likely with double-clicks, retries, or a code shared in a group chat. Fix by making the check and the mark-as-used one step that the database guarantees, for example a conditional update that only succeeds if the coupon is still unused, inside a transaction.

risks.title: Coupon is used up even if the order does not exist
risks.explanation: The discount is added to the order without first checking that the order exists. If the order number is wrong or missing, the update changes nothing, but the coupon is still marked as used. The customer then has a dead coupon and no discount. This can happen with a typo or a stale order number, and the customer gets no error. Fix by checking that the order exists before using the coupon, and doing both steps together so one cannot succeed without the other.

risks.title: One order can stack several coupons
risks.explanation: Nothing stops an order from taking a second or third coupon. Each one adds another $100 off the same total. A guest with several codes could pay much less than intended, and the total could go below what the product should cost. This is likely unintended unless the business has decided that coupons can stack. Fix by allowing only one coupon per order, or by stating the stacking rule and enforcing it.

questions_for_developer: If two requests use the same coupon code at the same moment, can both be accepted? Please make the check and the mark-as-used a single step that the database enforces, and test it with two simultaneous requests.
Should an order be allowed to use more than one coupon? If not, please block a second coupon on the same order.
Should the system confirm that the order exists, and is still unpaid, before it uses a coupon? Right now a coupon can be used up on an order number that does not exist.

Anyone who knows an order number and a coupon code can apply the coupon. Is that acceptable, or should the system check that the request comes from the buyer of that order? The payment step has the same gap, so this may need a wider fix.
good_news: The change is small and contained, touching only the new coupon file and one new route.
Invalid codes and used codes are rejected with a clear message instead of crashing.
The code cleans up spaces and capitals before the lookup, so typing mistakes are less likely to block valid codes.

results.title: 'Simplify middleware' drops /api/internal from the sign-in check; the revenue report route relied on it

findings.label: internal revenue/customer report API becomes reachable without signing in
findings.title: Customer names, emails and spending are now open to anyone

report.headline: A change removed the sign-in check from the internal revenue data, so anyone can now see customer details.
what_changed: The sign-in check that guarded the internal revenue data was removed for the web address that serves it. Anyone who visits that address without signing in now gets the data.
The data is a ranked list of every customer's name, email address and total lifetime spending.
The change also removed the sign-in check's special reply for unsigned requests to that address. Those requests now get sent to the sign-in page instead of a plain error.
The dashboard page still requires a staff sign-in. Its spelling fix ("bussiness" to "business") is correct and harmless.
The change's comment says the app's data pages check sign-in themselves. The revenue page does not, so the comment is wrong for it.

risks.title: Customer names, emails and spending are now open to anyone
risks.explanation: The internal revenue page returns every customer's name, email address and total spending. Its only protection was the sign-in check that this change removed, and the page has no sign-in check of its own. Anyone who finds the web address, which is easy to guess from the app's other addresses, can read the full list without signing in. Do not publish until a sign-in check is restored on that page.

questions_for_developer: Can you put the sign-in check back for the internal revenue web address before we publish, and confirm that an unsigned visit is refused?
Did anyone decide that the revenue page should be public? If not, why does the change say the page handles its own sign-in when it does not?
Is the staff sign-in check strong enough? It only confirms that a sign-in cookie exists and is longer than 20 characters, so could a visitor fake it?
good_news: The change is small and easy to reverse.
The spelling fix is correct and carries no risk.
The problem is found before release, so no customer data has been exposed yet.

results.title: 'Delete stale data' job removes accounts that haven't logged in for 90 days, including active subscribers

findings.label: paying subscribers who never log in get their accounts (and orders) permanently deleted
findings.title: Nightly job deletes paying subscribers who never log in

report.headline: A new nightly job would delete paying customers who have not logged in for 90 days, along with their subscriptions and orders.
what_changed: A new job runs every night at 3 AM and removes customer accounts that have not logged in for 90 days, or that have never logged in.
When an account is removed, the database also removes that customer's subscriptions and order history automatically.
The job also removes old login sessions that have expired. This part is harmless.
The stated reason is to lower the hosting bill. Removing customer accounts is unlikely to be the main driver of that cost, and the change does not show that it would be.

risks.title: Nightly job deletes paying subscribers who never log in
risks.explanation: The project notes say most subscribers never log in, because boxes ship and bill automatically. The new job removes every account with no login in 90 days or no login at all. Those accounts are often active, paying customers. Removing an account also removes its subscription, so weekly boxes stop and billing for those customers ends, starting with the first night the job runs. Because the job runs every night, the loss would keep growing. Do not ship this. Remove the new schedule line and get the owner's approval for any cleanup rule that excludes active subscribers.

risks.title: Order history is deleted along with the account
risks.explanation: Each customer's order records are linked to their account and are removed with it, so past payments and purchases would vanish from the database. Businesses often must keep payment and sales records for accounting or tax purposes for several years. Deleting them early could break those rules and make refund or dispute questions impossible to answer. This needs a check with whoever handles accounts and tax.

questions_for_developer: Will this job delete any account that has an active subscription? If yes, why is that intended?
Can deleted accounts, subscriptions and orders be restored from backups? If so, how long does a restore take?
Does the shipments table also delete rows when a subscription is removed? (It is not in the schema file we reviewed, so this could not be checked.)
Which time zone is the 3 AM run based on? Is it set to run when the fewest customers are active?
Is there a record-keeping rule that says how long order records must be kept, and does this job respect it?
good_news: The change is small and easy to undo. Removing the one line in the schedule file stops the job.
The part that removes expired login sessions does not affect customers or payments.

results.title: Config refactor inverts the free-shipping flag: free shipping for everyone unless explicitly turned off

findings.label: free shipping is now on by default (env var not set in production) so every order ships free
findings.title: Every order ships free unless a setting is explicitly turned off

report.headline: Shipping is now free on every order unless a setting is switched off, which would cost money in normal weeks.
what_changed: Free shipping is now the default for every order. Before this change, it was off unless someone turned it on.
To keep normal shipping charges, the setting must be set to "false". Leaving it unset now means customers pay no shipping at all.
The normal shipping rules are unchanged: a $5.99 flat fee, and free shipping on orders of $75 or more.
The change also moves the port, currency and shipping settings into one new file. The currency setting is added but nothing in this change uses it.

risks.title: Every order ships free unless a setting is explicitly turned off
risks.explanation: Before this change, free shipping only applied when someone deliberately switched it on. The new code reverses that: unless the setting is exactly "false", every order ships free. The project notes list only the port and the payment key as production settings, so nothing turns it off. Customers would then skip the $5.99 fee on every order, including orders under $75, and the company would absorb that cost until someone notices.

risks.title: A mistyped threshold value charges the flat fee on every order
risks.explanation: If the free-shipping threshold setting is set to something that is not a number, the code treats the threshold as missing. Every order then gets the $5.99 fee, including orders over $75. This is unlikely, because it only happens after a typing mistake in the setting, but customers would be overcharged and the mistake would be easy to miss.

questions_for_developer: Should free shipping be on all the time, or only during promo weekends as the project notes say? If only on promo weekends, please set the default back to off.
Before publishing, will the production setting for free shipping be explicitly set to "false"? If not, please change the default back so that unset means off.
Which pages or checkout steps call the shipping function? This repository only defines it and does not call it, so please confirm where customers see the shipping charge.
Can the threshold setting be checked when the app starts, so a bad value stops the publish instead of quietly charging every customer?
good_news: The change is small and contained, in two files.
The $5.99 fee and the $75 threshold keep the same values as before, so nothing else in the pricing changed.
Moving the settings into one file makes them easier to find and check.

results.title: Payment webhook stops verifying signatures 'temporarily'; anyone can mark orders as paid

findings.label: fake 'payment succeeded' messages can mark orders paid without paying
findings.title: Anyone can fake a payment and trigger free shipments

report.headline: The check that confirms payment notices are genuine was switched off, so fake payment messages can now mark orders paid and ship them.
what_changed: The address that receives payment notices from the payment provider no longer checks that each notice is genuine.
Any message sent to that address is now accepted as a real payment if it has the right shape.
A matching order is marked paid and sent to the print partner for fulfilment, as before.
Each incoming notice is now written to the log, including its type and order number.
The developer's stated reason is that a new load balancer changes the message, so the check failed. The check was turned off rather than fixed.

risks.title: Anyone can fake a payment and trigger free shipments
risks.explanation: The payment notice address now accepts messages from anyone on the internet, with no proof they came from the payment provider. Someone who knows or guesses an order number can send a fake 'payment succeeded' message. The order is then marked paid and sent to the print partner, so goods ship without payment. This is likely if order numbers are easy to guess, which we have not checked. Fix: restore the check and correct the load balancer so the original message reaches the app unchanged.

questions_for_developer: Can we turn the payment notice signature check back on before release, and fix the load balancer so it passes the original message through unchanged?
Can you show a test where a notice with a missing or wrong signature is rejected?
Are order numbers random and hard to guess, or are they simple counting numbers? If they are simple, can they be made random?
Does marking an order paid check that the amount received matches the order total? If not, can that check be added?
good_news: The change touches only one file, so the fix is contained.
The original check code still exists in the project, so restoring it should be quick.

results.title: Retry card charges on timeouts WITH the same idempotency key and only for network/5xx errors (safe twin of 04)

report.headline: Checkout now retries a failed card charge up to three times, using a protection against double charging.
what_changed: When a payment attempt fails because of a network problem, a timeout, or a temporary gateway error, checkout tries again, up to three times in total.
Each retry waits a little longer than the one before, starting at about a third of a second.
Every retry sends the same order reference to the payment provider, so the provider should not charge the customer twice for one order.
Other failures, such as a card being declined, are not retried and behave as before.
The payment provider's error type is now tracked so checkout can tell temporary failures from permanent ones.

risks.title: Checkout may wait up to about 25 seconds before showing a failure
risks.explanation: Each attempt waits up to 8 seconds before giving up, and there are three attempts. A customer on the checkout page could wait around 25 seconds before seeing a failure message, and may press Pay again. Pressing again reuses the same order reference, so it should not double charge, but the wait may feel slow. Consider a shorter overall time limit or a clear 'processing' message.

questions_for_developer: If all three attempts time out, the order is marked as failed, but the payment provider may still have completed the charge. Does the team have a process to check for and refund these orders? Can the order be marked as 'unknown' instead of 'failed' in that case?
Is the payment provider's documented repeat-request protection kept for long enough to cover our retry window, and has the team confirmed this with the provider?
Is a total wait of about 25 seconds acceptable for the checkout page, or should the total time be capped lower?
good_news: The change is small and contained to the payment step and one new helper file.
Every retry reuses the same order reference, which is the right way to guard against double charges.
Card declines and other permanent errors are not retried, so customers are not charged repeatedly for a refused card.

results.title: Drop users.legacy_avatar_url: replaced by avatar_key six months ago (values copied), no code reads it (safe twin of 05)

report.headline: The change permanently removes an old, unused avatar web address field from customer records, after the replacement image system already took over.
what_changed: Customer profiles no longer keep the old picture web address. Nothing in the app reads or writes that old address anymore.
A new change to how the database is organised removes that old address column for every customer.
Customers' profile pictures should look the same, because the app already uses the newer picture reference.
The old picture host was switched off in May, so the old web addresses already led nowhere.
The removal cannot be fully undone. The undo step adds the empty column back, but the old addresses would not come back.

risks.title: Full old picture addresses are permanently deleted
risks.explanation: The earlier change to the database only saved the file name from each old picture address, not the full address. This change deletes the full old addresses for all customers. Since the old picture host is already off, those addresses no longer work, so customers should see no difference. The only real harm is if someone later needs the full old addresses for a record or an audit. Ask a developer to confirm that no backup or export is needed before the change is published.

questions_for_developer: Before we publish, is there a backup or export of the old picture addresses, in case anyone needs them for records or audits later?
Does every customer who had an old picture address now have a picture file name saved in the new field? Please check a count before and after publishing.
The note in the earlier change says every old value was copied, but only the file names were copied. Should that note be corrected so future readers are not misled?
good_news: The change is small and contained: one field removed and one database step added.
Nothing else in the code uses the removed field, so no screen or feature should break.
The undo step is written, so the change can be reversed in structure if needed.

results.title: Product search gains category filter + sort using parameters and an allow-list (safe twin of 03)

report.headline: The product search can now be filtered by category and sorted by name or price, with safe handling of inputs.
what_changed: The product search page can now be narrowed to one category, such as a single product type.
Search results can be sorted by name (the default), lowest price first, or highest price first.
Any unknown sort option quietly falls back to sorting by name instead of returning an error.
Each search result now includes the product's category, which is a public catalogue detail.
Results are still capped at 50 products per search.
questions_for_developer: Does the shop's website or app use the new category and sort options yet, or is this only available to other software that calls the address directly?
Should products with the same price be ordered by name as a tie-breaker, so the order stays steady when prices match?
good_news: The change is small and contained to one file, and the sort options come from a fixed list, so user input cannot inject database instructions through sorting.
The category and price fields it relies on exist in the products table, so the search should not break.
The search terms and the category filter are kept separate from the database instructions, which is the safe way to handle customer-supplied input.

results.title: Request logging of method/path/status/duration only, no bodies, headers or query strings (safe twin of 08)

report.headline: The change adds a simple activity log for each web request, leaves out customer details, and looks safe to ship.
what_changed: Every request to the app now adds one line to the activity log. The line shows the action, the web address used, the result, and how long it took.
Customer details sent with requests, such as Social Security numbers and bank details, are deliberately kept out of this log.
Extra text after the question mark in a web address is also left out.
Staff will be able to see which requests fail and which are slow.
Each request now sends one more message to the outside log service, so the amount sent grows with traffic.

risks.title: Outside log service bill grows with every request
risks.explanation: Each visit to the app now sends one more message to the outside log service (Better Stack). Those services often charge by volume, so costs rise as traffic rises. This is small and expected, but it should be watched. Check the log service's usage and bill after release.

risks.title: Requests that crash may leave no log line
risks.explanation: The new log line is written only after the app finishes a request. If a request crashes with an unhandled error, no line is written, which weakens the goal of seeing which calls fail. This does not affect customers, but failures may be harder to diagnose. Ask the developer whether crashed requests should also be logged.

risks.title: Future web addresses could carry personal data into the logs
risks.explanation: The full web address is logged. The only address today is the loan application page, which carries no customer ID, so no personal data reaches the logs now. If a future address includes a customer's name or ID, that detail would be sent to the outside service and kept for about 30 days. Developers should keep personal details out of web addresses.

questions_for_developer: Can you test whether the existing log-sending setup sends its own internal messages back into itself, which could flood the log service and raise our bill? Please confirm before we add more logging.
Can you make sure requests that crash with an error still get a log line, so we can see failures?
Is our outside log service approved to hold loan-related business names and loan amounts for about 30 days? Can a business name ever be a person's full name?
If we add customer IDs to web addresses later, can we keep them out of the logs?
good_news: The change is small and contained: 29 lines in three files, and it is easy to undo.
The new log line deliberately leaves out request bodies, headers and search text, which is the right privacy choice for loan applications.
The only web address today takes no customer ID, so no personal details reach the new log lines.
